sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In 490 BCE an Achaemenid expedition under Datis and Artaphernes crossed the Aegean and reached Attica.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The expedition sought to subdue Athens and Eretria. These were imperial objectives, wider than a single battlefield.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Athens needed to preserve its independence; the expedition needed political submission as well as military success.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Marathon was a coastal plain in northeastern Attica. Herodotus describes it as suitable for cavalry.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Athenian and Plataean infantry opposed the Persian expedition. Athenian command included Miltiades and the polemarch Callimachus.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Herodotus describes stronger Greek wings and a shallower center. This is a literary account, not a surveyed deployment.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The narrative moves from an advance to fighting in the center, success on the wings, and a struggle near the ships.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Committing to battle involved accepting risk without certainty about Persian intentions. The surviving narrative cannot recover a commander's private reasoning.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Greek wings prevailed while their center gave ground; the wings then converged against the remaining Persian troops.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Persian force withdrew by sea. The Athenians returned to protect Athens.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The battle became a durable civic memory: the Marathon museum preserves finds associated with the Athenian and Plataean burial mounds.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Compare battlefield success with the continuing task of defending the city. A successful engagement does not remove every operational threat.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Persian cavalry activity and exact troop positions are unresolved here. Accounts of Datis's fate conflict; a schematic must not imply certainty.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Read Herodotus as a later Greek narrative, Iranica for Datis and source criticism, and the archaeological museum for material context.

phases.title: Opposing armies
phases.description: The expedition and Greek defenders face one another on the Marathon plain.

phases.title: Center under pressure
phases.description: In Herodotus's account, the Persian center advances against the thinner Greek center.

phases.title: Wings converge
phases.description: The successful Greek wings turn toward the remaining enemy.

phases.title: Return to Athens
phases.description: The defenders return while the Persian fleet sails around the coast.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Cannae followed Roman defeats at the Trebia and Lake Trasimene during Hannibal's invasion of Italy.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Fabius had avoided favorable battle conditions for Hannibal. The consuls of 216 BCE instead commanded a major concentration of Roman forces.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Rome sought a decisive battlefield recovery; Hannibal sought another defeat severe enough to weaken Roman resistance.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The armies fought near the Aufidus river in Apulia. Polybius reports that Paullus judged the open, level ground unfavorable because Hannibal was stronger in cavalry.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Hannibal commanded African, Iberian, Celtic and Numidian contingents. Roman consuls were Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Polybius describes a projecting Iberian-Celtic center with African infantry on either side; both armies placed cavalry on their wings.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Cavalry fighting accompanied the infantry collision. Roman pressure bent Hannibal's center inward before the Africans attacked the Roman flanks.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Concentration against the enemy center made sense as a breakthrough attempt, but success there did not guarantee security on the flanks.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Victorious Carthaginian cavalry returned against the Roman rear while infantry closed from the sides.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Roman army suffered a catastrophic defeat. Paullus died; Varro survived.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Rome continued the war. Livy's epitome records emergency recruitment and the refusal to ransom prisoners.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Cannae separates tactical achievement from strategic resolution: destroying an army did not compel the Roman state to surrender.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Ancient casualty totals differ. Livy's hostile portrayal of Varro should not be treated as a neutral record of responsibility or private motives.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Polybius supplies the core battle narrative. Livy provides another tradition, read here in translation and through the periochae. The Cambridge edition's introduction explains Livy's life, composition and how his text survives.

phases.title: Formation
phases.description: The opposing infantry centers and cavalry wings deploy.

phases.title: Roman advance
phases.description: The Roman infantry presses into the Iberian-Celtic center.

phases.title: Envelopment
phases.description: African infantry turns inward; cavalry threatens the Roman rear.

phases.title: Army defeated
phases.description: Roman resistance collapses, but Rome continues the war.

perspectives.name: Hannibal Barca
perspectives.objective: Defeat the concentrated Roman army.
perspectives.known: His own army combined infantry contingents with strong cavalry.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the center could remain coherent under pressure.
perspectives.constraints: A multinational army required coordination across separate arms.
perspectives.decision: The ancient narratives describe a yielding center and attacks from the flanks. This explanation reconstructs the plan; it is not a surviving order.
perspectives.forces: A multinational army of African, Iberian and Celtic infantry with Iberian, Celtic and Numidian cavalry. Polybius reports it was outnumbered in infantry; ancient totals are uncertain.
perspectives.terrain: Open ground near the Aufidus favored his stronger cavalry, while the river limited the Romans' room to extend their line.
perspectives.logistics: Far from Carthage, he lived on what he could take in Italy. Before the battle he seized the Roman supply depot at Cannae.
perspectives.outcome: The Roman army was destroyed, but Rome refused to negotiate. Later admiration for the battle as a model of envelopment can obscure that Hannibal lost the war.

perspectives.name: Gaius Terentius Varro and Lucius Aemilius Paullus
perspectives.objective: Bring Hannibal to a decisive engagement.
perspectives.known: Rome had assembled a large infantry force after earlier defeats.
perspectives.uncertainty: The effect of Hannibal's deployment and the cavalry contest.
perspectives.constraints: Shared consular command and pressure to reverse Roman losses.
perspectives.decision: They fought a pitched battle. Livy assigns the initiative to Varro, but his moral contrast between the consuls requires caution.
perspectives.forces: A very large Roman and allied army, strongest in heavy infantry and weaker in cavalry. Ancient figures for its size differ.
perspectives.terrain: Polybius reports that Paullus considered the open plain unfavorable against Hannibal's cavalry.
perspectives.logistics: A large concentrated army needed steady supply, and Hannibal's capture of the Cannae depot added pressure to act.
perspectives.outcome: A catastrophic defeat in which Paullus died. Ancient writers assigned blame along political lines, especially against Varro.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In 52 BCE Vercingetorix's forces occupied Alesia during the resistance to Caesar's conquest of Gaul.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Caesar's account presents Roman command from the conqueror's perspective. Political self-presentation shapes the narrative.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Romans sought surrender by siege; the defenders awaited a relief army.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Caesar describes a hilltop settlement, nearby rivers, a plain and surrounding heights. The museum interprets the site at Alise-Sainte-Reine.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Caesar directed Roman legions and cavalry; Vercingetorix led the besieged force. Several Gallic leaders shared command of the relief army.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Roman works faced both the settlement and the approaching relief force.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Investment was followed by relief attempts, attacks from inside and outside, and the defeat of the relieving army.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Caesar reports moving reserves to threatened sectors and sending cavalry around the outer works.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: In his narrative, Roman reinforcement and a cavalry attack in the rear broke the final external assault.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Vercingetorix surrendered. Caesar distributed many prisoners as enslaved captives.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The result strengthened Roman domination while imposing conquest and captivity on the defeated population.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Study siege engineering together with food supply and coordination. Static fortifications still required decisions about mobile reserves.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Enemy numbers and dramatic speeches come from Caesar's interested account. The displayed phases simplify an extended siege, not a measured hour-by-hour reconstruction.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Caesar supplies the principal narrative; museum archaeology and landscape interpretation provide a different kind of evidence.

phases.title: Investment
phases.description: Roman works close around Alesia.

phases.title: Double front
phases.description: The Romans prepare to defend against forces outside and inside.

phases.title: Relief assaults
phases.description: The relief army attacks while the besieged attempt sorties.

phases.title: Surrender
phases.description: Vercingetorix is surrendered and the defenders lose their freedom.

perspectives.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
perspectives.objective: Force the surrender of Vercingetorix's army before a Gallic relief force could break the siege.
perspectives.known: Vercingetorix had sent his cavalry out to summon a relief army from across Gaul.
perspectives.uncertainty: When the relief force would arrive and where it would attack.
perspectives.constraints: Food and fodder for his legions, and long lines to man against two fronts at once.
perspectives.forces: Roman legions with allied cavalry, including Germanic horsemen.
perspectives.terrain: The hilltop settlement, its rivers and the surrounding heights set the course of the works. A weak point on the outer line became the focus of the final assault.
perspectives.logistics: He gathered supplies to sustain the army inside its lines.
perspectives.decision: He built inner and outer lines and, in the final assaults, moved reserves to threatened sectors and sent cavalry outside the works. The record of these decisions is Caesar's own.
perspectives.outcome: Vercingetorix surrendered. Caesar's narrative presents the victory as his personal achievement.

perspectives.name: Vercingetorix and the Gallic relief commanders
perspectives.objective: Hold Alesia until a relief army could break the Roman lines from outside.
perspectives.known: Food in the settlement was limited, and a relief army was being raised across Gaul.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the relief army would arrive before supplies ran out.
perspectives.constraints: Coordinating attacks from inside and outside the Roman lines without reliable communication.
perspectives.forces: The besieged army in the settlement and a relief army under several commanders, including Vercassivellaunus.
perspectives.terrain: Roman works blocked access across the plain and the surrounding hills.
perspectives.logistics: Caesar reports that the Mandubii, inhabitants of Alesia, were expelled to save food and were refused passage through the Roman lines.
perspectives.decision: Breakouts were timed with the relief army's assaults. After those failed, Vercingetorix surrendered. Gallic decisions are known almost entirely through Caesar.
perspectives.outcome: Surrender, captivity and enslavement for many of the defeated.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Edward the Confessor's death opened a disputed succession. Harold became king; William of Normandy claimed the crown.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Harold defeated the Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge before returning south to face William's landing in Sussex.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: William needed to defeat the reigning king to advance his claim. Harold needed to contain an invader while preserving royal authority.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The English held a ridge near the modern town of Battle. The battlefield's exact extent remains uncertain.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Harold's army fought on foot, including household warriors. William's army used infantry, archers and mounted troops.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The English occupied the ridge in a defensive formation; William's forces approached from rising ground to the south.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Repeated assaults lasted throughout 14 October 1066. A Norman retreat and rally preceded renewed attacks.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: William rallied his troops after a report that he had died. English pursuit during retreats exposed parts of their formation.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The interaction of lost cohesion and repeated pressure matters more than explaining the result through a single weapon.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Harold was killed and his army broken. William was crowned on Christmas Day.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The victory opened the Norman conquest and transformed England's political relationship with continental Europe.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Distinguish an army's tactical position from the wider demands of defending a kingdom against successive invasions.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The Bayeux Tapestry and written narratives leave details unresolved. This account does not specify Harold's exact fatal wound or precise unit positions.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: English Heritage summarizes the narrative and material setting. Historic England documents the registered battlefield and surviving source problems.

phases.title: The ridge
phases.description: Harold's infantry holds the higher ground.

phases.title: Assault and rally
phases.description: William's forces attack; the duke restores confidence during a retreat.

phases.title: Repeated pressure
phases.description: Further attacks and pursuits disrupt sections of the English formation.

phases.title: Collapse
phases.description: Harold's death accompanies the defeat of his army.

perspectives.name: William, Duke of Normandy
perspectives.objective: Defeat Harold in battle to make good his claim to the English crown.
perspectives.known: Harold had come south after Stamford Bridge, and the English held a strong position on a ridge.
perspectives.uncertainty: How long the English shield wall could hold, and whether his own army would stay together under repeated repulses.
perspectives.constraints: An invading army in hostile country, dependent on its ships and on foraging.
perspectives.forces: Norman, Breton and other French troops, combining infantry, archers and mounted warriors.
perspectives.terrain: His army attacked uphill from rising ground to the south of the English position.
perspectives.logistics: The army was sustained from its base near Hastings and by foraging in Sussex.
perspectives.decision: He launched repeated assaults and, in the narratives, rallied his troops after a rumor of his death. Whether later Norman retreats were deliberate feints is debated.
perspectives.outcome: Harold was killed and his army broken. William was crowned on Christmas Day 1066.

perspectives.name: Harold II of England
perspectives.objective: Defeat or contain the invasion and preserve his kingship.
perspectives.known: William had landed at Pevensey. Harold's own army had just fought at Stamford Bridge in Yorkshire.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether more troops would join him if he waited, and what William would do in the meantime.
perspectives.constraints: Losses and fatigue after Stamford Bridge and a hurried march south.
perspectives.forces: Household warriors and other troops fighting on foot in a shield wall.
perspectives.terrain: The ridge gave a strong defensive position but little room to maneuver.
perspectives.logistics: The rapid march from Yorkshire left little time to gather fresh forces.
perspectives.decision: He gave battle quickly near Hastings instead of waiting for a larger army. Historians debate whether he meant to fight at once or to pin William near the coast.
perspectives.outcome: His death and the collapse of his army opened the way to the Norman conquest.

sources.title: 2 décembre 1805 : La bataille d'Austerlitz
sources.publisher: French Ministry of the Armed Forces

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The 1805 campaign carried the Grande Armée from the Channel camps through the Ulm campaign and into Austria.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Austria and Russia confronted Napoleon within the Third Coalition. The battle took place on 2 December 1805 in present-day Czechia.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Napoleon sought a decisive result before the coalition could improve its position. The Allies attempted to turn the French right.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Pratzen Heights dominated the battlefield; Telnitz and Sokolnitz lay in the southern sector.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: French corps under commanders including Soult, Davout and Lannes faced a combined Austro-Russian army.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Allied formations occupied the heights before moving substantial forces south against Napoleon's right.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The southern fighting developed first. Soult then attacked the weakened center, followed by fighting for the plateau and an Allied retreat.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Napoleon committed Soult against the Pratzen Heights as Allied troops moved away.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Control of the center divided the coalition's fight and allowed the French to redirect forces against its southern wing.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The French won decisively. Austria signed an armistice on 6 December.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Treaty of Pressburg followed on 26 December, reshaping the political settlement after the campaign.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A useful study question is how timing, terrain and concentration interacted. A deliberate risk can only be assessed against the forces available to support it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The popular image of a perfectly controlled trap compresses a contested battle. This overview omits disputed losses and exact minute-by-minute timing.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Fondation Napoléon timeline and site guide supply sequence and geography. The French Army page represents an institutional commemorative interpretation.

phases.title: Allied movement south
phases.description: Allied forces advance toward Telnitz and Sokolnitz.

phases.title: Assault on Pratzen
phases.description: Soult's corps attacks the weakened Allied center.

phases.title: Contest for the center
phases.description: Counterattacks fail to restore Allied control of the plateau.

phases.title: Allied withdrawal
phases.description: The divided Allied army retreats; French forces press its southern wing.

perspectives.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
perspectives.objective: Win a decisive battle before Prussia joined the coalition and before further Allied reinforcements arrived.
perspectives.known: The Allies had advanced toward him and occupied the Pratzen Heights, which he had left to them. An attack on his right was expected.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether reinforcements marching from the south would arrive in time to hold the southern sector, and when the Allies would weaken their center.
perspectives.constraints: A long line of communication through Austria after the Ulm campaign, and an army that was smaller on the field until its corps concentrated.
perspectives.forces: Corps including those of Soult, Lannes, Bernadotte and Davout, with the Guard and Murat's cavalry.
perspectives.terrain: The Pratzen plateau dominated the center. Streams, ponds and the villages of Telnitz and Sokolnitz shaped the southern fighting.
perspectives.logistics: Far from France, the army needed a quick decision rather than a prolonged campaign in Moravia.
perspectives.decision: He held Soult's corps ready and launched it against the Pratzen Heights once Allied columns had moved south, around 8–8:30 a.m. in the sources. This describes observable decisions, not his private thoughts.
perspectives.outcome: A decisive French victory, followed by an Austrian armistice on 6 December. The image of a perfectly controlled trap compresses a hard-fought battle.

perspectives.name: Allied command: Kutuzov, Weyrother and the allied emperors
perspectives.objective: Turn the French right and cut Napoleon's communications with Vienna.
perspectives.known: French forces appeared weaker on their right, and the Allies held the Pratzen plateau.
perspectives.uncertainty: The true strength and position of the French army, including forces arriving from the south.
perspectives.constraints: A divided command with Alexander I and Francis I present, and a complex plan requiring several columns to march across the plateau.
perspectives.forces: A combined Russian and Austrian army organized in several attack columns.
perspectives.terrain: Moving off the Pratzen plateau to support the southern attack left the center exposed.
perspectives.logistics: Supplies in Moravia were strained. Waiting for reinforcements and for Prussia was an alternative some favored.
perspectives.decision: They committed most columns to the southern attack, weakening the center. Accounts differ on Kutuzov's reservations about the plan; they are not reconstructed here.
perspectives.outcome: Defeat split the army and Austria left the war. Russian and Austrian accounts later blamed each other.

sources.title: Three plans showing the Battle of Waterloo, 1815 (MPH 1/387)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Napoleon returned from Elba in 1815. A new coalition mobilized against him.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: His advance into Belgium sought to separate Wellington's and Blücher's armies before larger coalition forces arrived.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The French needed a rapid decision; the Allies needed to sustain cooperation despite separate command structures.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Wellington held the Mont-Saint-Jean ridge with forward strongpoints including Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Napoleon faced Wellington's multinational army and, later, Blücher's Prussian corps.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Much Allied infantry sheltered behind the crest of the ridge, out of sight and partly protected from artillery. Squares formed against the later cavalry attacks.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Attacks on the strongpoints and center were followed by cavalry assaults, Prussian intervention and the final Guard attack.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Wellington chose to stand with promised Prussian support. Blücher marched toward him after the defeat at Ligny.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Prussian pressure forced Napoleon to divide attention and reserves. The Imperial Guard's repulse preceded general French retreat.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The coalition won on 18 June. Napoleon's attempt to restore his rule failed.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The campaign ended with Allied occupation of Paris and Napoleon's final exile.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Coalition cooperation can be an operational capability. Study liaison and marching decisions alongside the actions visible on the battlefield.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: National narratives assign credit differently, including the weight given to the Prussian intervention. The schematic simplifies simultaneous engagements and is not derived from period maps.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Compare the National Army Museum narrative with Royal Armouries and the Prussian-focused Fondation Napoléon dossier. The National Archives holds three 1815 plans of the battle (MPH 1/387); they are catalogued but not digitised.

phases.title: Strongpoints attacked
phases.description: French assaults begin against Wellington's forward positions.

phases.title: Assaults on the ridge
phases.description: Infantry and cavalry fighting tests the Allied line.

phases.title: A second front
phases.description: Prussian forces enter the battle against Napoleon's right.

phases.title: Final repulse
phases.description: The Guard attack fails; the Allied advance and pursuit follow.

perspectives.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
perspectives.objective: Defeat Wellington before the coalition armies could combine effectively.
perspectives.known: Ligny had forced a Prussian retreat, but its direction and recovery remained critical.
perspectives.uncertainty: How much Prussian force could reach the battlefield in time.
perspectives.constraints: Wet ground, elapsed time and competing demands for reserves.
perspectives.decision: He continued the attack while allocating troops to the Prussian threat. The account describes actions, not an invented inner monologue.
perspectives.forces: The Army of the North, strong in artillery and cavalry, with the Imperial Guard as a final reserve. Grouchy's wing had been detached to follow the Prussians.
perspectives.terrain: Rain-soaked ground delayed the attack and hampered artillery and cavalry. Fortified farms broke up assaults before they reached the ridge.
perspectives.logistics: The campaign had to succeed quickly, before larger coalition armies reached France's frontiers.
perspectives.outcome: Defeat ended his return to power. Debate continues over the late start, Grouchy's movements and the use of the cavalry and the Guard.

perspectives.name: Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington
perspectives.objective: Hold the position until Prussian assistance could make a combined victory possible.
perspectives.known: Blücher had promised support; his arrival depended on a difficult march.
perspectives.uncertainty: The timing and scale of reinforcement.
perspectives.constraints: A mixed army, an extended defensive line and repeated French pressure.
perspectives.decision: He defended the ridge and strongpoints, then advanced as the French attack failed.
perspectives.forces: A multinational army of British, Dutch-Belgian, Hanoverian, Brunswick and Nassau troops of uneven experience.
perspectives.terrain: The Mont-Saint-Jean ridge sheltered infantry behind its crest. Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte broke up attacks in front of the line.
perspectives.logistics: His communications ran north toward Brussels and the coast. Contact with the Prussians was essential to the plan.
perspectives.outcome: A combined Allied victory. British national narratives long underplayed the Prussian contribution.

perspectives.name: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher
perspectives.objective: Restore cooperation with Wellington after Ligny.
perspectives.known: Wellington intended to fight near Waterloo.
perspectives.uncertainty: March delays and the situation when each corps arrived.
perspectives.constraints: Reorganization after defeat and routes from Wavre.
perspectives.decision: He committed corps toward Waterloo. Their intervention turned a two-army encounter into a coalition victory.
perspectives.forces: Prussian corps regrouping after Ligny. Bülow's corps, which had not fought at Ligny, led the march to Waterloo.
perspectives.terrain: Muddy lanes slowed the march from Wavre. Plancenoit became the focus of the Prussian attack on the French right.
perspectives.logistics: Retreating north to Wavre after Ligny, rather than east toward Prussia, kept the army in reach of Wellington while it regrouped.
perspectives.outcome: The Prussian attack and pursuit turned the French defeat into a rout. Some national narratives have underestimated this role.

sources.title: Major Fleet-versus-Fleet Operations in the Pacific War, 1941–1945

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After rapid Japanese expansion, the Combined Fleet planned an operation against Midway in June 1942.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Yamamoto hoped to draw American carriers into a decisive engagement. U.S. intelligence identified Midway as the principal objective.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Japan sought a favorable fleet battle; Nimitz sought to protect Midway while exploiting advance warning.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The engagement spread across open ocean around the atoll. Scouting aircraft connected widely separated forces.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Nagumo led four Japanese fleet carriers. Fletcher and Spruance commanded three American carriers under Nimitz's operational direction.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: American carrier groups waited northeast of Midway; the Japanese carrier force approached to support the island attack.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The 4 June island strike was followed by unsuccessful American attacks, devastating dive-bomber strikes and Japanese counterattacks.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Fletcher authorized Spruance's early strike while retaining aircraft pending better information. Nagumo faced conflicting demands to rearm aircraft and recover the island strike.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: American dive bombers disabled three Japanese carriers in the morning; Hiryu was mortally damaged later that day.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Japan abandoned the invasion. Four Japanese carriers and the American Yorktown were lost.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The result materially altered the carrier balance, but did not end the Pacific War.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Intelligence created opportunity without removing uncertainty. Scouting, carrier deck operations, navigation and command decisions shaped whether it could be exploited.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: A simple luck-versus-genius explanation obscures interacting causes. The schematic illustrates sequence, not verified ship tracks.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: NHHC provides chronology and intelligence context; the Naval War College study supports analysis of command decisions and incomplete information.

phases.title: Midway attacked
phases.description: Japanese carrier aircraft strike the atoll.

phases.title: Search and launch
phases.description: American aircraft attack; both sides act on incomplete contact reports.

phases.title: Carrier crisis
phases.description: Dive bombers inflict fatal damage on Akagi, Kaga and Soryu.

phases.title: Counterattack and withdrawal
phases.description: Hiryu counterattacks before its loss; Japan withdraws and Yorktown is subsequently lost.

perspectives.name: Chester W. Nimitz and the American carrier command
perspectives.objective: Defend Midway and attack the approaching carrier force.
perspectives.known: Communications intelligence indicated the objective, approximate timing and force.
perspectives.uncertainty: Contact reports did not initially locate every enemy carrier.
perspectives.constraints: Three carriers, aircraft range and the time needed to launch and recover strikes.
perspectives.decision: Nimitz concentrated carriers near Midway; Fletcher and Spruance launched attacks based on scouting reports. These were decisions under uncertainty, not omniscient ambush management.
perspectives.forces: Three carriers, Enterprise, Hornet and the hastily repaired Yorktown, supported by land-based aircraft on Midway.
perspectives.terrain: Open ocean. Weather, distance and aircraft range governed when and where strikes could be launched.
perspectives.logistics: Yorktown's rapid repair after Coral Sea added a third carrier to the American force.
perspectives.outcome: Four Japanese fleet carriers were sunk and Yorktown was lost. Interpretations range from emphasizing intelligence to stressing the contingency of strike timing.

perspectives.name: Chūichi Nagumo
perspectives.objective: Support the Midway operation while retaining capacity to strike enemy ships.
perspectives.known: The first attack reported a need for another island strike; later scouting identified American ships.
perspectives.uncertainty: The enemy's carrier strength and immediate intentions.
perspectives.constraints: Rearming, landing returning aircraft and defending the carriers competed for time.
perspectives.decision: He ordered preparations for another island strike before new contact information changed the situation. Reasons are reconstructed from operational records rather than private thoughts.
perspectives.forces: Four fleet carriers, Akagi, Kaga, Sōryū and Hiryū, with the main battleship force far to the rear.
perspectives.terrain: Operating within range of Midway's aircraft exposed his carriers to repeated attacks from the island as well as the American carriers.
perspectives.logistics: Flight decks could not at once recover the island strike, rearm aircraft and launch against ships; each choice took time.
perspectives.outcome: All four carriers were lost. Postwar accounts, including the story that the carriers were five minutes from launching, have been revised by later research.

sources.title: A Soviet mortar team advance at Stalingrad, 1942

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Germany's 1942 southern offensive aimed toward the Caucasus oilfields and the Volga region after the failure to defeat the Soviet Union in 1941.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Army Group South was divided, creating competing demands between the Caucasus and Stalingrad.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The campaign combined resource objectives with control of a major transport corridor. Reducing it to a contest over the city's name is inadequate.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Stalingrad extended along the Volga. The surrounding steppe remained essential to the wider battle.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Paulus commanded the German Sixth Army. Soviet defense included the 62nd Army under Chuikov; Romanian formations held exposed sectors outside the city.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: German forces advanced toward the Volga while Soviet forces defended the approaches and then the urban area.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The campaign moved from the summer advance through urban fighting to Operation Uranus and the destruction of the encircled force.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Soviet learning and organizational reform helped make the counteroffensive possible; no single commander's personality adequately explains it.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The November Soviet offensive broke through the flanks and encircled the Sixth Army.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The remaining German forces surrendered by 2 February 1943.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The defeat damaged German strategic prospects and became a major psychological turning point.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Examine an urban battlefield inside its operational setting. Tactical advances through a city can coexist with growing vulnerability outside it.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: German and Soviet postwar narratives both simplified responsibility. Casualty totals depend on whether they cover the city, encirclement or wider campaign.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National WWII Museum emphasizes Soviet adaptation; USHMM places the defeat in the war's broader course. NAM supplies additional operational context.

phases.title: Advance to the Volga
phases.description: German forces push toward Stalingrad amid Soviet resistance.

phases.title: Urban battle
phases.description: Fighting narrows the Soviet foothold but does not end resistance.

phases.title: Operation Uranus
phases.description: Soviet attacks against the flanks encircle the German army.

phases.title: Final surrender
phases.description: The encircled force is defeated in separate pockets.

perspectives.name: Friedrich Paulus and the German Sixth Army command
perspectives.objective: Take Stalingrad and secure the Volga flank of the German southern offensive.
perspectives.known: By autumn most of the city had been taken. The flanks were held by Romanian, Hungarian and Italian armies.
perspectives.uncertainty: The strength of Soviet forces gathering beyond the flanks.
perspectives.constraints: Overstretched supply lines, and orders from Hitler that limited withdrawal and, later, a breakout.
perspectives.forces: The Sixth Army, worn down by months of fighting in the city.
perspectives.terrain: Ruined city blocks favored defenders, while the open steppe beyond the flanks was thinly held.
perspectives.logistics: After the encirclement, air supply could not sustain the army, and its strength declined through December and January.
perspectives.decision: He kept fighting in the city and, once encircled, did not break out against orders. Whether a breakout was feasible remains debated.
perspectives.outcome: Surrender by 2 February 1943. About 91,000 survivors went into captivity.

perspectives.name: Soviet command: Chuikov's 62nd Army and the Stavka planners
perspectives.objective: Hold the city to fix German forces in place while preparing a counteroffensive against the flanks.
perspectives.known: German strength was concentrated in the city, and the flanks were held by weaker allied armies.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the 62nd Army could hold its shrinking strip along the river until the counteroffensive was ready.
perspectives.constraints: Reinforcements had to cross the Volga under fire, and the offensive had to be prepared in secret.
perspectives.forces: The 62nd Army in the city, and fronts to the north and south strengthened by newly formed tank and mechanized corps.
perspectives.terrain: A narrow strip along the Volga inside the city, and open steppe for the encirclement.
perspectives.logistics: River crossings sustained the defense, while the counteroffensive required concentrating forces without detection.
perspectives.decision: The 62nd Army fought a layered, small-unit defense, and Operation Uranus struck the flanks in November. Credit for planning Uranus is disputed in memoirs.
perspectives.outcome: Encirclement and destruction of the Sixth Army, at very great cost to soldiers and civilians.

sources.title: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 3.8–15 (trans. E. J. Chinnock)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After his earlier victories over Persian armies, Alexander moved from the Mediterranean coast into Mesopotamia in 331 BCE. Darius III had meanwhile assembled a new army drawn from across his empire, each contingent under its own commander.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Alexander lingered in Tyre and other cities while Greek affairs, including the rising of Agis III of Sparta, demanded attention. Darius made a further peace offer, which Alexander rejected. Reinforcements Alexander expected from Europe never arrived, possibly because Antipater needed them against Agis.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Darius sought a battle on open ground where his numbers, cavalry and scythed chariots could be used, having been persuaded that the narrow field at Issus had cost him. Alexander needed to defeat the king's army in the field to make good his claim to rule Asia.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The armies met on a broad plain near Gaugamela, north-west of Arbela (modern Erbil). Arrian reports that the Persians had long before levelled the uneven ground so that chariots and cavalry could move freely. The exact site cannot be fixed with certainty.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Persian army combined many regional contingents, Greek mercenaries, a few Indian elephants and scythed chariots. Arrian's reported Persian totals are not credible counts, and Livius gives no totals. Alexander commanded the Companion cavalry on the right; Parmenion commanded the left wing.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Darius stood in the centre with his kinsmen and guard. Bactrian and Scythian cavalry under Bessus, with chariots in front, faced Alexander's right, while Greek mercenaries faced the phalanx. Alexander placed a second line behind the first, with orders to face about if the army were surrounded, and set angled flank guards on both wings.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The Macedonians crossed the Tigris largely unopposed in mid-September, and a lunar eclipse followed on about 20 September. The Persian army spent the night before the battle under arms. On 1 October Alexander edged to the right, a cavalry fight developed on that flank, the chariots were neutralized, and Alexander then charged the Persian centre.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Arrian reports that Alexander rejected Parmenion's advice to attack at night, citing the risks of night fighting in unfamiliar country. Darius, fearing a surprise attack, kept his army standing in formation overnight. During the battle Darius sent cavalry around the Macedonian right to halt Alexander's movement.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: As Persian cavalry was drawn into the fight on Alexander's right, a gap opened in the Persian front. Alexander formed a wedge of Companions and nearby infantry and drove toward Darius. The opportunity arose from the Persians' own outflanking effort rather than from a fixed plan.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Darius fled and his army dispersed. Alexander turned back to help Parmenion's hard-pressed wing, then pursued to Arbela, where he took the royal treasure and Darius's chariot but not the king himself. The Babylonian diary records that the king's troops deserted him.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The battle decided the fate of the Achaemenid empire. A contemporary Babylonian diary calls the victor "king of the world", and Darius escaped to Media intending to raise another army.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Preparing ground for one arm can tie an army to that ground. Alexander's second line, ordered to face about if surrounded, shows how a reserve can protect against the breakthroughs a broad enemy line makes likely.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Dust hid much of the fighting, so its exact course is unknown. Arrian says Darius fled first, while the contemporary diary says his troops abandoned him; Livius prefers the diary. Greek accounts may also carry Macedonian propaganda, and their troop and casualty figures are unreliable.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Arrian's narrative draws on earlier accounts, citing Aristobulus for the captured Persian order of battle. Livius sets the Greek tradition beside the Babylonian Astronomical Diaries, which date the eclipse and the battle independently.

phases.title: Approach and omens
phases.description: The Macedonians cross the Tigris; a lunar eclipse unsettles the Persian army.

phases.title: Drift to the right
phases.description: Alexander edges right; Persian cavalry rides around his flank and the scythed chariots are neutralized.

phases.title: The gap
phases.description: Persian cavalry is drawn away; Alexander's wedge strikes toward Darius, who flees.

phases.title: Left wing and pursuit
phases.description: Parmenion's wing is pressed and the camp raided; Alexander returns, then pursues to Arbela.

perspectives.name: Alexander III of Macedon
perspectives.objective: Destroy Darius's new army in battle and with it the king's authority.
perspectives.known: Captured Persian riders reported that Darius was near. The Persians held a broad plain prepared for cavalry and chariots.
perspectives.uncertainty: The Persian line far overlapped his own, and he could not know whether his wings would hold against envelopment.
perspectives.constraints: Expected reinforcements from Europe had not arrived. In Arrian's account he judged a night attack too risky in country the enemy knew better.
perspectives.forces: The Macedonian phalanx, Companion cavalry, Thessalian and allied cavalry, and light troops such as Agrianians and archers.
perspectives.terrain: Open, levelled ground that favoured the larger Persian cavalry and the chariots.
perspectives.logistics: A fortified camp, with the baggage guarded by Thracian infantry; it was raided during the battle.
perspectives.decision: He refused a night attack, built a second line and angled flank guards, edged to the right and charged into the gap in the Persian front.
perspectives.outcome: Darius fled, but a call for help from Parmenion drew Alexander back, and the king escaped to Media.

perspectives.name: Darius III of Persia
perspectives.objective: Fight on open ground where numbers, cavalry and scythed chariots could be used, unlike the narrow field at Issus.
perspectives.known: Alexander had crossed the Euphrates and Tigris and was approaching the prepared battlefield.
perspectives.uncertainty: When and how Alexander would attack; Arrian says he feared a night assault.
perspectives.constraints: An army of many peoples under their own commanders, whose morale Livius describes as shaken by the eclipse and other omens.
perspectives.forces: Regional cavalry from Bactria, Media, Parthia and elsewhere, Greek mercenaries, a few elephants and scythed chariots.
perspectives.terrain: A broad plain he had chosen and levelled for his chariots.
perspectives.logistics: His base at Arbela held treasure and royal property, which fell to Alexander after the battle.
perspectives.decision: He kept his army under arms overnight, sent cavalry around Alexander's right and launched the chariots against the phalanx.
perspectives.outcome: When Alexander's charge reached his centre he fled, or in the Babylonian account was abandoned by his troops, and escaped east.

sources.title: The Chronicles of Enguerrand de Monstrelet, vol. 4 (trans. Thomas Johnes)
The soldier in later medieval England and the battle of Agincourt

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In 1415 Henry V of England invaded Normandy and besieged and took Harfleur. He then resolved to march through northern France to English-held Calais.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Henry pressed a claim to the French throne, which the victory later strengthened. The French king summoned men-at-arms from across the kingdom, and a royal council resolved to give battle, while France's princes remained divided by their own conflicts.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Henry needed to bring his army safely to Calais. The French aimed to intercept and destroy it before it got there.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Barred from the Somme ford at Blanchetaque, the English crossed further upstream and were met near Azincourt. They advanced from Maisoncelles over fields recently sown with corn, with Tramecourt to one side. Record-based research argues the ground could not have held the very large French army of popular accounts.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Anne Curry's study of English and French financial records suggests roughly 8,500–9,000 English and about 12,000 French, a much smaller gap than the chronicles imply. Most of Henry's army were archers, and Welsh soldiers were a small share. The French command was shared among the constable, the marshal and several great princes.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Monstrelet describes the French in a vanguard, main body and rearguard, with mounted wings to strike the English flanks. The vanguard was led by the constable with the dukes of Orléans and Bourbon and Marshal Boucicaut. The English placed archers in front, each with a sharpened stake, men-at-arms behind and horses and baggage to the rear.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On Friday 25 October the French waited by their banners. The English advanced and opened with heavy archery. A French mounted attack on the flanks failed, and wounded horses recoiled into the vanguard. Close fighting followed, then a raid on the English baggage, the killing of prisoners and the withdrawal of the French rear.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The French chose to wait for an attack, confident in their numbers, although Monstrelet says some leaders privately feared an open battle. Henry advanced to bring on the fight. When the baggage was attacked and a renewed assault seemed possible, he ordered the prisoners killed.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The failed mounted attack disordered the French vanguard. Pressed together, it could fight only with its front rank, while English archers and men-at-arms struck it.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The English won. Monstrelet lists many French princes and lords among the dead and captured. Henry withdrew to Maisoncelles, then marched to Calais and embarked for England.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The victory supported Henry's claim to the French throne. The battle later became central to English and British national memory, shaped above all by Shakespeare's Henry V.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Archery from a protected position mattered most against an enemy that was crowded and disordered. The size of an army counted for less than whether it could use its numbers.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Army sizes remain debated: chronicles give far larger French totals than the administrative records. Ransom contracts suggest the killing of prisoners did not spare men by rank. The archers' V sign has no contemporary record, and the Welsh did not form most of the army.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Monstrelet gives a detailed French narrative, but figures such as his 13,000 English archers conflict with record evidence. University of Southampton research uses muster rolls, pay records and ransom contracts to test the chronicles.

phases.title: The armies draw up
phases.description: The French form three divisions and wait; English archers plant stakes in front of the line.

phases.title: English advance
phases.description: The English move forward and open heavy archery; the French mounted flank attack fails.

phases.title: Close combat
phases.description: Recoiling horses disorder the crowded French vanguard, which is defeated hand to hand.

phases.title: Alarm and killing of prisoners
phases.description: A raid on the baggage leads Henry to order prisoners killed; the French rear withdraws.

perspectives.name: Henry V of England
perspectives.objective: Bring his army from Harfleur to Calais and uphold his claim in France.
perspectives.known: A French army had gathered across his route after he was forced away from the Somme ford at Blanchetaque.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the French would attack or simply block his road, and whether his outnumbered army could survive a battle.
perspectives.constraints: An army that had besieged Harfleur and then detoured upstream to cross the Somme, far from its base.
perspectives.forces: Mainly archers with a smaller body of men-at-arms; record evidence suggests about 8,500–9,000 men.
perspectives.terrain: Open fields recently sown with corn between Maisoncelles, Azincourt and Tramecourt.
perspectives.logistics: Horses and baggage were kept to the rear, where a French raid struck them.
perspectives.decision: He advanced to provoke an attack, with archers protected by stakes, and later ordered the prisoners killed when a renewed attack seemed possible.
perspectives.outcome: A decisive victory, after which he continued to Calais and returned to England.

perspectives.name: Charles d'Albret, constable of France
perspectives.objective: Stop the English army before it reached Calais, as the royal council had resolved.
perspectives.known: The English army was smaller and had been marching through hostile country.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether waiting or attacking would serve better; Monstrelet says some leaders privately feared an open battle.
perspectives.constraints: Command of the vanguard was shared with royal dukes and other great lords. This analysis infers rather than documents how far that limited his authority.
perspectives.forces: Men-at-arms, archers and crossbowmen in three divisions with mounted wings; record evidence suggests about 12,000 men.
perspectives.terrain: Recently sown fields where the vanguard became crowded once the fighting began.
perspectives.logistics: Men-at-arms summoned from across the kingdom to intercept the English march.
perspectives.decision: The French waited in position, then sent mounted wings against the English flanks before the vanguard closed.
perspectives.outcome: The vanguard was defeated; Monstrelet lists many French princes and lords killed or captured.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By 1863 the Union had gained ground on most fronts: Grant was besieging Vicksburg and the navy was blockading Southern ports. The Eastern Theater remained the Confederacy's main success, and after victory at Chancellorsville in May Lee decided to invade the North.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The National Park Service describes Lee's aims as raising Confederate morale, easing pressure on Vicksburg, drawing the Union army onto better ground, gathering supplies from Pennsylvania farms and winning victories that might push the Union toward peace.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Lee's plan included destroying the Susquehanna bridge at Harrisburg and disabling the Pennsylvania Railroad. Lincoln and Halleck ordered the Army of the Potomac to stay between Lee and Washington; on 28 June George Meade replaced Joseph Hooker in command.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: After 1 July the Union held high ground south of the town in a fishhook-shaped line from Culp's Hill through Cemetery Hill and Cemetery Ridge to Little Round Top. The Confederates formed a longer, outer arc along Seminary Ridge about a mile away, with open fields between.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Lee commanded the Army of Northern Virginia, with corps under Longstreet, Ewell and Hill. Meade commanded the Army of the Potomac, which he had led for only a few days. Stuart's cavalry was out of contact with Lee as the armies converged.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Learning that Union forces had crossed the Potomac, Lee concentrated near Cashtown, west of Gettysburg. Heth's division approached along the Chambersburg Pike while Buford's Union cavalry approached from the south. Neither commander expected to fight at Gettysburg.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 1 July Confederates attacked on McPherson Ridge and drove Union troops through the town to Cemetery Hill. On 2 July Lee attacked both Union flanks. On 3 July Union troops retook works on Culp's Hill, a two-hour bombardment preceded an assault on the Union centre, and that assault failed. Lee withdrew from 4 July.

refs.locator: The Third Day; End of Invasion

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: At midnight on 2 July Meade's corps commanders advised holding their positions, and he did. Having found the Union flanks strong, Lee attacked the centre on 3 July with about 12,000 men in what became known as Pickett's Charge.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: On the high ground, the Union's shorter interior line let Meade shift troops to threatened points, while Confederate attacks from the outer arc were harder to coordinate. The failure of the 3 July assault ended Lee's hope of victory on this field.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Lee began an orderly retreat late on 4 July, with a long train of wounded. Heavy rain slowed both armies, and the swollen Potomac trapped Lee until the river fell and he crossed into Virginia. Critics charged that Meade had let the Confederate army slip away.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Gettysburg's churches, public buildings and homes became hospitals. A Soldiers' National Cemetery was established, and Lincoln spoke at its dedication on 19 November 1863. The war continued until Lee surrendered at Appomattox in April 1865.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An unplanned meeting engagement can commit whole armies to ground neither commander chose. Lee's loss of cavalry reconnaissance shows how gaps in information shape decisions before the fighting starts.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Park Service pages describe Lee's aims with different emphases, and their figures are approximations. Meade's pursuit remains debated. This study does not adopt labels such as "high-water mark" or repeat casualty totals.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National Park Service overview and teaching background give the campaign and the three days. The park's historical handbook adds the plan of campaign, Meade's council of war and the retreat.

phases.title: Meeting engagement
phases.description: Confederates attack west of town and drive Union troops back to Cemetery Hill.

phases.title: Attacks on both flanks
phases.description: Longstreet strikes the Union left and Ewell the right; the Union line holds.

phases.title: Assault on the centre
phases.description: After a bombardment, about 12,000 Confederates advance on Cemetery Ridge and are repulsed.

phases.title: Retreat
phases.description: Lee withdraws toward Virginia; Meade pursues but Lee crosses the Potomac when the river falls.

perspectives.name: Robert E. Lee
perspectives.objective: Win a decisive victory on Northern soil that would raise Confederate morale and press the Union toward peace.
perspectives.known: On the night of 28 June an agent reported that the Union army had crossed the Potomac and was close.
perspectives.uncertainty: With Stuart's cavalry out of contact, he had little reconnaissance of Union strength and positions.
perspectives.constraints: A supply line stretched far from Virginia, and corps that had to concentrate quickly from scattered positions.
perspectives.forces: The Army of Northern Virginia, with corps under Longstreet, Ewell and Hill.
perspectives.terrain: Seminary Ridge, an exterior line facing open fields toward the Union centre.
perspectives.logistics: The army foraged in Pennsylvania farmland; its retreat began with a wagon train of wounded many miles long.
perspectives.decision: He attacked both Union flanks on 2 July and, finding them strong, attacked the centre on 3 July.
perspectives.outcome: The assault failed, and he retreated to Virginia.

perspectives.name: George G. Meade
perspectives.objective: Keep the Army of the Potomac between Lee and Washington and defeat the invasion.
perspectives.known: He took command on 28 June at Frederick, Maryland, only days before the battle.
perspectives.uncertainty: Where Lee would strike next; before 3 July he expected the main attack on his left.
perspectives.constraints: New to army command, with corps arriving at Gettysburg piecemeal after the first day.
perspectives.forces: The Army of the Potomac, whose corps commanders he consulted in a midnight council of war.
perspectives.terrain: High ground in a fishhook-shaped interior line from Culp's Hill to Little Round Top.
perspectives.logistics: Reserve batteries were brought up behind the centre, and the Baltimore Pike ran behind the Union right.
perspectives.decision: He held his positions and kept three corps on his left, while Hancock strengthened the stone wall at the centre; after the battle he pursued Lee.
perspectives.outcome: A defensive victory, followed by criticism that Lee had been allowed to escape.

sources.title: D-Day: The Allied Invasion of Normandy
World War II: D-Day, The Invasion of Normandy

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By spring 1944 Germany had dominated western Europe for four years; Anglo-American offensives in North Africa and the Mediterranean had ruled out an earlier return to northern France. Allied conferences in 1943 shaped the invasion plan, and Eisenhower was appointed to command it in December 1943.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Allies considered a second front in north-west Europe essential to defeating Germany and to relieving pressure on the Soviet Union. Hitler's Directive No. 51 ordered the western defences reinforced, and he hoped that defeating an invasion would free forces for the Eastern Front.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Allies aimed to land, establish a lodgement including Caen, then break out and liberate France. German commanders disagreed over how to defeat them: Rommel wanted to fight on the beaches, while Geyr von Schweppenburg wanted to hold armour back for a mass counterattack.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Normandy was chosen over the shorter crossing to Calais for its beaches, weaker defences and position within fighter range. The Atlantic Wall was nearly continuous only in the Pas de Calais. Inland, enclosed bocage country favoured the defenders.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Eisenhower was Supreme Allied Commander, with Montgomery commanding the ground forces. On the German side, Rundstedt commanded in the west and Rommel led Army Group B. Hitler split the panzer reserve: Rommel controlled three divisions, and four could not move without Hitler's permission.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Americans landed at Utah and Omaha, British troops at Gold and Sword, and Canadians at Juno, with airborne forces on both flanks. Static divisions of uneven quality held most of the coast, but the veteran 352nd Infantry Division, undetected by Allied intelligence, defended Omaha. Only 21st Panzer was within striking distance.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Airborne landings and bombardment preceded the beach assaults on 6 June. Cherbourg fell on 27 June and St-Lô on 19 July, while British and Canadian attacks ground forward around Caen. Operation Cobra broke through from 25 July. The German counterattack at Mortain on 7 August failed, and the Falaise Pocket closed in the third week of August.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Eisenhower launched the invasion in a spell of bad weather that made the decision fraught; he had drafted a press statement for use if it failed. Hitler refused withdrawal and ordered the Mortain counterattack, which exposed his armies to encirclement.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Deception held the German Fifteenth Army in the Pas de Calais. Repeated British and Canadian attacks drew most German armour to Caen, leaving the western sector weaker for the American breakout.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Allies were established in France. The Falaise Pocket was sealed in late August; many Germans escaped without their equipment, but Seventh Army and Fifth Panzer Army had effectively ceased to exist. The campaign ended with the liberation of Paris on 25 August.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The campaign opened the way to the liberation of France and the advance into Germany. The war in Europe continued until Germany's unconditional surrender, signed at Reims on 7 May 1945.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Combined operations depend on deception, air superiority and supply as much as on the assault. D-Day missed many first-day objectives, including Caen, yet put more than 160,000 troops ashore and secured a foothold.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Casualty figures differ between and even within institutional accounts. The date the Falaise Gap closed is given as 19, 21 or 22 August, depending on whether the link-up or the end of resistance is meant. Imperial War Museums credits German defensive skill while doubting any strategy could have changed the outcome.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National Army Museum covers planning and the landings. Imperial War Museums gives the German command debate and campaign. The Eisenhower Library holds planning and command documents, and Veterans Affairs Canada summarizes the Canadian part of the campaign.

phases.title: Landings
phases.description: Airborne drops, bombardment and assaults on five beaches establish a foothold.

phases.title: Battle for the lodgement
phases.description: Cherbourg falls; British and Canadian attacks around Caen hold German armour in the east.

phases.title: Breakout
phases.description: Operation Cobra breaks through in the west; the German counterattack at Mortain fails.

phases.title: Falaise Pocket
phases.description: Allied armies close the pocket around German forces; Paris is liberated on 25 August.

perspectives.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
perspectives.objective: Land Allied armies in France, build up the lodgement and defeat German forces in the west.
perspectives.known: Air reconnaissance, special forces and the French Resistance had mapped much of the German coastal defence.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the weather would allow the landing, and whether it would succeed; he drafted a statement in case it failed.
perspectives.constraints: A short weather window and a multinational coalition of land, sea and air forces.
perspectives.forces: More than 5,000 ships, airborne divisions and assault divisions from several nations, with Montgomery commanding on land.
perspectives.terrain: Beaches of varying strength, then enclosed bocage country inland.
perspectives.logistics: Southern England was packed with men, vehicles and supplies; by 30 June over 850,000 men had landed.
perspectives.decision: He launched the invasion on 6 June despite the uncertain weather.
perspectives.outcome: The landings succeeded, and by late August the campaign had broken German resistance in Normandy.

perspectives.name: Erwin Rommel
perspectives.objective: Defeat the invasion on the beaches.
perspectives.known: Invasion was imminent, and Allied air superiority would make it hard to move armour once the battle began.
perspectives.uncertainty: Where the main landing would fall; deception convinced the German high command that Normandy was a feint.
perspectives.constraints: He controlled only three panzer divisions, and four more could not move without Hitler's permission.
perspectives.forces: Army Group B, with Seventh Army in Normandy and Brittany and Fifteenth Army north of the Seine.
perspectives.terrain: An Atlantic Wall that was incomplete outside the Pas de Calais, which he strengthened with obstacles and mines.
perspectives.logistics: Air attacks held up fuel, ammunition and reinforcements.
perspectives.decision: He pushed for armour near the coast and strengthened the beach defences; he was away in Germany when the landings began.
perspectives.outcome: German resistance contained the Allies for weeks but could not throw them back. Rommel was badly wounded on 17 July.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By late 1915 the German chief of staff, Erich von Falkenhayn, believed Germany could not win by military strength alone. He planned to defeat France before British forces were fully deployed, hoping a major French defeat would push its politicians toward peace.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Verdun was chosen in December 1915. Its forts had been stripped of guns in August 1915, its supply routes were limited, and the city combined military value with national pride: French leaders declared that morale would not survive its loss.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Imperial War Museums describes Falkenhayn's concept as using more than 1,200 guns to destroy French units on ground they had to retake, while committing German infantry sparingly. The French aimed simply to hold Verdun.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The fortress city lay on the River Meuse, ringed by 19 forts, of which Douaumont was the largest and highest. Heights on the east (right) bank dominated the area; the Mort-Homme and Hill 304 lay on the west bank. A single road from Bar-le-Duc carried most French supply.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The German Fifth Army attacked under Crown Prince Wilhelm, with General Schmidt von Knobelsdorf an influential adviser. The French Second Army was commanded from 26 February by Philippe Pétain and later by Robert Nivelle, under Joffre as commander-in-chief.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: French positions north of the city were thin. Lieutenant-Colonel Driant, who had warned of the weak defences, held woods in the path of the attack with about 1,200 light infantry; only around a hundred survived unhurt.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: A massive bombardment opened the battle on 21 February 1916, and Fort Douaumont fell on 25 February. Germany attacked the west bank from 6 March, took Fort Vaux on 7 June and reached Fort Souville on 11–12 July before being pushed back. French counteroffensives retook Douaumont on 24 October and Vaux in November, and the battle ended in December.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Pétain defended in depth with mutually supporting strongpoints, rotated divisions through the battle in a system called the noria and greatly increased French artillery. Crown Prince Wilhelm's staff, by contrast, made seizing ground the priority rather than Falkenhayn's limited concept.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Once both armies fought for ground rather than to destroy the other's units, losses fell equally on both. The Somme offensive from late June then forced Germany to reduce its effort at Verdun and let Nivelle attack.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: France held Verdun and recovered Douaumont, Vaux and much of the lost ground. Falkenhayn's plan to destroy the French army had failed.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Verdun's losses, added to those of the Somme, created a German manpower crisis. In France the battle became the national symbol of the Great War. Nine villages were destroyed and never rebuilt, and the Douaumont Ossuary holds the remains of about 130,000 soldiers.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An attritional plan depends on controlling the objective. When commanders pursue ground for its own sake, the attacker can suffer as heavily as the defender.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Falkenhayn's postwar claim that he meant to bleed the French army white is debated; other readings stress the capture of the town or drawing in Allied reserves. The sources differ on the start of the bombardment (4 a.m. or 7.15 a.m.), the end date (15 or 18 December) and when Pétain left (late April or May).

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Mémorial de Verdun gives a detailed French chronology, logistics and memory. Imperial War Museums gives the strategic concept and the changing German conduct of the battle.

phases.title: Opening bombardment
phases.description: German artillery overwhelms the right-bank positions; Fort Douaumont falls.

phases.title: Both banks
phases.description: Germany attacks the Mort-Homme and Hill 304 and takes Fort Vaux.

phases.description: German attacks reach Fleury and Fort Souville before the Somme draws resources away.

phases.description: French counteroffensives retake Douaumont and Vaux and push the line back.
