perspectives.known: French losses in 1914–1915 had been heavy, and Verdun's forts had lost their guns in August 1915.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether the French would defend Verdun at any cost, and whether his subordinates would keep to a limited, artillery-led attack.
perspectives.constraints: Germany's limited manpower, and an army command that pursued the capture of ground.
perspectives.forces: The Fifth Army under Crown Prince Wilhelm with more than 1,200 guns.
perspectives.terrain: Heights on the east bank of the Meuse that dominated the city and its forts.
perspectives.logistics: Verdun's limited supply routes appeared to favour the attacker.
perspectives.decision: He launched an artillery-heavy offensive on the east bank on 21 February and extended it to the west bank in March.
perspectives.outcome: The plan failed. German losses at Verdun and the Somme together produced a manpower crisis.

perspectives.name: Philippe Pétain
perspectives.objective: Hold Verdun and stabilize a collapsing front.
perspectives.known: When he took command on 26 February, much of the right bank had been overrun and Fort Douaumont had fallen.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether a single supply road could sustain the defence under constant shelling.
perspectives.constraints: The Mémorial de Verdun says Joffre moved him in spring because he demanded too many resources.
perspectives.forces: The French Second Army, with steadily increased artillery.
perspectives.terrain: Ground suited to a defence in depth of mutually supporting strongpoints.
perspectives.logistics: The Voie Sacrée from Bar-le-Duc carried about 90,000 men and 50,000 tonnes of equipment a week.
perspectives.decision: He defended in depth, rotated divisions through the battle and kept the supply road open.
perspectives.outcome: Verdun held. He was succeeded by Nivelle, whose later counterattacks recovered much of the lost ground.

sources.title: El Alamein: outfoxing the “Desert Fox”, 1942
sources.publisher: AWM London (Australian Department of Veterans' Affairs)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Italy invaded Egypt from Libya in 1940, and Germany intervened in 1941. In 1942 Rommel defeated the British at Gazala and took Tobruk on 21 June, and Commonwealth forces fell back to a line at El Alamein.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The First Battle of El Alamein in July and Rommel's failed attack at Alam Halfa on 30 August stopped the Axis advance. Churchill wanted a victory before the Allied landings in North-West Africa and pressed for an early attack; Montgomery, commanding Eighth Army since August, refused until he was ready.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Montgomery aimed to break the Axis position and destroy its army. Short of fuel and mechanized forces, Rommel aimed to hold a deep defensive position.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Alamein line ran from the Mediterranean to the Qattara Depression, which tanks could not cross, so neither flank could be turned. The Axis protected its positions with deep minefields that Rommel called the "devil's gardens".

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Eighth Army drew troops from across the British Empire, including Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, with Greek, Polish and French contingents, and clearly outnumbered the German and Italian army in men, tanks and guns. Alexander was Commander-in-Chief Middle East.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Axis infantry and armour held positions in depth behind the minefields. The 9th Australian Division held the northern end of the Allied line near the coast.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Operation Lightfoot opened on the night of 23 October with a heavy barrage, and infantry and engineers attacked to open corridors through the minefields. A week of attritional fighting followed, with Australian attacks in the north. Operation Supercharge began on the night of 1–2 November, and the Axis line broke on 4 November.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Montgomery built up men, training and equipment before attacking. When armour stalled in the minefield corridors, he continued an attritional phase he called "crumbling", made a diversionary attack to draw in Axis reserves and paused to regroup before Supercharge.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Australian drive toward the sea pulled Axis forces north and unbalanced them. Continued attrition used up Rommel's scarce reserves before Supercharge struck.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: By late afternoon on 4 November the Axis army was in full retreat. Most of its infantry was captured, but Montgomery's caution let the motorized elements escape, and the British pursued into Libya.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: El Alamein was the British Army's first clear, decisive victory over the Axis. Four days later the Torch landings began, and Axis forces in North Africa surrendered in Tunisia in May 1943.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Deliberate preparation and material superiority can overcome a prepared defence, but only through costly attrition, and a cautious exploitation may let a beaten enemy escape.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The National Army Museum suggests Churchill's "end of the beginning" framing may overstate the battle's strategic weight, and Montgomery's conduct remains debated. The two sources give different force totals, and disagree on whether Lightfoot opened corridors through the minefields in its first hours.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The National Army Museum gives the British strategic and command narrative and its debates. AWM London gives the Australian 9th Division's role and the RAAF's support.

phases.title: Crumbling
phases.description: Attritional fighting wears down Axis armour; Australian attacks draw Axis forces north.

phases.description: New Zealand and British troops attack again; the Axis line breaks on 4 November.

phases.title: Pursuit
phases.description: Axis infantry is captured, but motorized units escape west into Libya.

perspectives.objective: Break the Alamein position and defeat the Axis army decisively.
perspectives.known: The Axis was short of fuel and mechanized forces and had built deep minefields.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether armour could pass through narrow minefield corridors under anti-tank fire.
perspectives.constraints: Churchill's pressure for an early victory before the Allied landings in North-West Africa.
perspectives.forces: Eighth Army, drawn from across the British Empire with Greek, Polish and French contingents, superior in men, tanks, guns and aircraft.
perspectives.terrain: A front between the sea and the Qattara Depression, with no open flank to turn.
perspectives.logistics: Weeks of build-up in men, tanks, guns and aircraft before the attack.
perspectives.decision: He delayed until ready, persisted with attrition when the armour stalled, and launched Supercharge after regrouping.
perspectives.outcome: The breakthrough came on 4 November, but the Axis motorized units escaped.

perspectives.name: Erwin Rommel
perspectives.objective: Hold the Alamein position against a stronger enemy.
perspectives.known: Eighth Army was building up superior forces opposite him.
perspectives.uncertainty: Where the main British blow would fall.
perspectives.constraints: Shortages of fuel and mechanized forces.
perspectives.forces: German and Italian infantry and armour, outnumbered in men, tanks and guns.
perspectives.terrain: Deep minefields he called the "devil's gardens", covering a line that could not be outflanked.
perspectives.logistics: Fuel shortages limited how freely he could move his armour.
perspectives.decision: He defended in depth and counterattacked; his reserves were drawn north and worn down.
perspectives.outcome: His army retreated on 4 November; most of the infantry was captured, but motorized units escaped.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the defeat at Stalingrad in February 1943, Hitler persisted with an offensive in the east despite concerns from commanders such as Guderian. Manstein urged an attack on the Kursk salient, a Soviet bulge between Orel and Belgorod.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Hitler delayed the operation, code-named Citadel, until July to build up armour and assault guns. It became the last major German offensive on the Eastern Front.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Germans aimed to attack the salient from north and south. The Soviet high command (Stavka) expected the attack and planned to absorb it in deep defences before launching powerful counteroffensives.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The salient extended about 160 miles from north to south and 100 miles from east to west. In the south, the German advance culminated near Prokhorovka.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Both sides concentrated vast forces, with the Soviets holding a clear numerical advantage and a reserve front behind the salient. Manstein commanded the German southern attack. Totals differ substantially between the sources.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Soviet forces built up to six belts of fortifications. Good intelligence, possibly including Enigma intercepts passed on by the British, helped them anticipate the attack.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The German attack began on 5 July. It stalled in the north with slight gains and culminated in the south near Prokhorovka on 11–12 July. A Soviet counteroffensive toward Orel began on 12 July, a second in the south followed from 3 August, and the campaign ended with the capture of Kharkov on 23 August.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Stavka chose to defend first and counterattack later. After the Allied landing in Sicily on 10 July, Hitler told his generals on 12 July that he wanted to move troops to Italy; Menning writes that he diverted the II SS Panzer Corps and ordered Manstein onto the defensive.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Defences in depth absorbed the German attack before it broke into open country, leaving the attackers worn down when the Soviet counteroffensives began.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: For the first time, a German offensive failed to achieve a breakthrough. Soviet counteroffensives took Orel and Kharkov, and the strategic initiative passed permanently to the Soviet side.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Germany could no longer mount a major offensive in the east. For the Red Army, Kursk showed mature coordination of several fronts and effective defence in depth, at an immense human cost to both sides.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Intelligence, prepared depth and well-placed reserves let a defender choose when to shift to the offensive.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Western accounts long relied on German sources, and Menning writes that the full intelligence story "remains to be told". The figures for forces and losses cited by the museum, from David Glantz and Karl-Heinz Frieser, differ widely from Menning's. The label "largest tank battle in history" depends on how the fighting is counted.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Menning's encyclopedia entry gives the operational narrative and historiography. The National WWII Museum article sets out the battle's scale and the Soviet counteroffensive.

phases.title: Prokhorovka

phases.title: Belgorod–Kharkov
phases.description: A southern counteroffensive breaks through and takes Kharkov, ending the campaign.

perspectives.known: The salient between Orel and Belgorod offered a target for attacks from north and south.
perspectives.uncertainty: How strong the Soviet defences had become during the months of delay.
perspectives.constraints: Hitler controlled the timing, and after the Sicily landings he withdrew forces and ordered a defensive posture.
perspectives.forces: German armies and armour concentrated for the southern attack; the sources' totals differ.
perspectives.terrain: Defended belts across the southern face of the salient, with the advance culminating near Prokhorovka.
perspectives.logistics: The delay was used to build up armour and assault guns.
perspectives.decision: He pressed the southern attack from 5 July until it was halted near Prokhorovka.
perspectives.outcome: Ordered onto the defensive, his forces then lost Kharkov to the Soviet counteroffensive in August.

perspectives.name: Stavka (Soviet high command)
perspectives.objective: Absorb the expected German attack, then launch decisive counteroffensives.
perspectives.known: Intelligence indicated a German attack on the salient, possibly aided by Enigma intercepts passed by the British.
perspectives.uncertainty: When the attack would begin, since Hitler delayed it until July.
perspectives.constraints: The need to hold the salient long enough to wear down German armour before committing reserves.
perspectives.forces: Several fronts with a numerical advantage and a reserve front behind the salient.
perspectives.terrain: Up to six belts of field fortifications across the salient.
perspectives.logistics: Reserves and fresh forces were assembled for counteroffensives in the north and south.
perspectives.decision: It defended first, then attacked toward Orel from 12 July and toward Kharkov from 3 August.
perspectives.outcome: The German offensive failed, and the strategic initiative passed permanently to the Soviet side.

sources.title: Dien Bien Phu & the Fall of French Indochina, 1954
sources.publisher: Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The Viet Minh had fought French forces in northern Vietnam since 1946. The United States, alarmed by communist movements in Asia after 1949, funded the French war. In May 1953 General Henri Navarre took command in Indochina, charged with finding an honourable way out.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Navarre's two-year plan was discussed in Paris but never formally approved, and he received no clear answer on what to do if Laos were threatened. The announcement in February 1954 of a Geneva conference raised the stakes, and Chinese aid to the Viet Minh increased sharply.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Navarre meant the base to protect Laos, draw Viet Minh forces away from the Tonkin delta and support operations. The Viet Minh concentrated to destroy the garrison.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The base lay in a valley near the Laotian border. Its key element was the airfield, surrounded by strongpoints with women's names such as Béatrice, Gabrielle, Anne-Marie and Huguette.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Colonel de Castries commanded a garrison of twelve battalions. General Giap concentrated several Viet Minh divisions, with artillery and anti-aircraft regiments, around the valley.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: French and Vietnamese paratroopers dropped into the valley on 20–22 November 1953 in Operation Castor and built an air-ground base. By the end of December the garrison was encircled, while Viet Minh troops dug trenches and tunnels toward its positions.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Viet Minh artillery opened fire on 13 March 1954. Béatrice and Gabrielle fell within two days, and the airstrip could not be used after 26 March. Fighting for the eastern hills lasted from 30 March to 10 April. The final offensive began on 1 May, and resistance ended on 7 May.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: France reinforced the shrinking garrison by parachuting in volunteers, many of them not trained parachutists. Washington would intervene only as part of a coalition, and Britain and other NATO members declined to join.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The loss of the airfield left a garrison designed around air supply dependent on parachute drops, while the Viet Minh tightened the ring.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Late on 7 May, de Castries ordered the fighting to stop. About 10,000 men were taken prisoner; the French ministry states that around 60 per cent of them died in Viet Minh camps.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Geneva agreements of July 1954 brought a ceasefire and a temporary division of Vietnam at the 17th parallel, with elections planned for 1956. The United States did not sign the second agreement and backed Ngo Dinh Diem in the South. French rule in Indochina ended.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A base that depends on a single airfield is only as secure as that airfield. An opponent who can bring supplies to a remote place should not be underestimated.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The U.S. Office of the Historian counts a four-month siege, from the encirclement; the French ministry dates the battle from the 13 March attack. Navarre's unapproved plan leaves responsibility for the decision open, and Viet Minh losses are historians' estimates.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The French Ministry of the Armed Forces gives the plan, the course of the siege and its human cost. The U.S. Office of the Historian gives American deliberations and the Geneva settlement.

Excerpts from The Red Cliff, Part I, by Su Shi

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: As Han authority collapsed, regional warlords fought for control. By 208 Cao Cao held the North China plain and turned south against Liu Biao, Governor of Jing province, and Sun Quan, who controlled the lower Yangzi.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: De Crespigny notes that when the Later Han was founded, control of the North China plain had decided the civil war, and in 208 most people, including Cao Cao's opponents, expected the pattern to repeat. When Liu Biao died that autumn, his successor Liu Zong surrendered Jing province.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Cao Cao occupied the naval base at Jiangling and called on Sun Quan to surrender. De Crespigny suggests he probably saw the advance as an armed reconnaissance that he could abandon if it failed. Sun Quan sent troops forward to test Cao Cao's strength while keeping a reserve with which to negotiate.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The armies met at the Red Cliffs on the Yangzi, between present-day Wuhan and Yueyang. The northern troops were unused to southern waterways and marshland. The precise site remains debated; the cliff where Su Shi's boat party of 1082 took place was only traditionally identified with the battle.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Sun Quan's power was a fraction of what Cao Cao could mobilize, but his Yangzi navy was experienced and locally superior. Zhou Yu commanded Sun Quan's forces alongside Liu Bei. Much of Cao Cao's fleet had served Liu Biao, and its loyalty was uncertain. Cao Cao's claim of about 800,000 men is not credible.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Liu Bei tried to hold a line on the Yangzi but was caught and heavily defeated, and turned to Sun Quan. His lieutenant Guan Yu had saved much of the Jing fleet. The allies and Cao Cao's forces then faced each other across the river for several days.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Cao Cao took over Jing province in autumn 208 and pursued Liu Bei eastward with his army and new fleet. At the Red Cliffs his first attack was driven back. When the wind changed, Zhou Yu sent in fireships, and Cao Cao abandoned his position and retreated, leaving garrisons. The following year Zhou Yu captured Jiangling.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: After debate at his headquarters, Sun Quan chose to fight rather than surrender. Zhou Yu used the change of wind for a fire attack, a common weapon of the time, and Cao Cao chose to withdraw rather than fight on.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The fire attack struck an army already worn by forced marches, sickness and uncertain loyalties. A setback became a retreat because Cao Cao's force was not fit for a prolonged river campaign.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Cao Cao retreated north. The allies, in de Crespigny's words, enhanced their victory with tales of slaughter, and Zhou Yu took Jiangling the next year.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The south kept naval control of the middle Yangzi, and later northern attempts to break the river defences failed. De Crespigny judges that the campaign proved to be the last chance for many years to reunite the empire, opening the way to the Three Kingdoms.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Control of a great river and skill on it could offset a large difference in overall strength. An advance meant as a probe can still decide a war if it fails.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: De Crespigny considers Cao Cao's defeat probably exaggerated and the story embellished by later literature, above all the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (chapters 43–50). Popular retellings add episodes such as a chained fleet and Huang Gai's feigned defection, which this study does not treat as established.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The main historical account is the biography of Zhou Yu in the Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi), with Pei Songzhi's commentary. De Crespigny's history is the principal source here; World History Encyclopedia reflects the popular tradition, and Su Shi's essay shows how the battle was remembered.

phases.title: Alliance on the river
phases.description: Sun Quan sends Zhou Yu to join Liu Bei; the armies face each other across the Yangzi.

phases.title: Fire attack
phases.description: Cao Cao's first attack fails; with a change of wind, fireships drive him from his position.

phases.title: Retreat and Jiangling
phases.description: Cao Cao withdraws north, leaving garrisons; Zhou Yu captures Jiangling the following year.

perspectives.known: Jing province had surrendered with its fleet, and Liu Bei had been heavily defeated.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether Sun Quan would surrender, and whether the former Jing troops and sailors would stay loyal.
perspectives.constraints: Troops tired by a long campaign and forced marches, unused to southern waterways and suffering from sickness.
perspectives.forces: His northern army and the fleet taken over from Liu Biao; his claim of about 800,000 men is not credible.
perspectives.terrain: The middle Yangzi and its marshlands.
perspectives.logistics: The captured naval base at Jiangling.
perspectives.decision: He pursued eastward with army and fleet and demanded Sun Quan's surrender, probably treating the advance as an armed reconnaissance.
perspectives.outcome: Driven from his position by a fire attack, he retreated and lost Jiangling the following year.

perspectives.name: Sun Quan
perspectives.objective: Preserve his independent state on the lower Yangzi.
perspectives.known: Cao Cao had taken Jing province and its naval base and was advancing downriver.
perspectives.uncertainty: Whether to fight or submit; his headquarters debated the choice at length.
perspectives.constraints: A power only a fraction of Cao Cao's, with an exposed northern flank and inaccessible hill country in the south.
perspectives.forces: An experienced Yangzi navy commanded by Zhou Yu.
perspectives.terrain: The river itself, where his fleet held local superiority.
perspectives.logistics: Control of the Yangzi below Wuhan, the Poyang region and Hangzhou Bay.
perspectives.decision: He sent Zhou Yu forward to join Liu Bei and test Cao Cao's strength, keeping a reserve with which to negotiate if necessary.
perspectives.outcome: Victory secured southern control of the middle Yangzi for many years.

sources.title: Al-Baladhuri: The Battle of the Yarmuk (636) and After

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the Ridda Wars reasserted the caliphate's control of Arabia, Muslim armies advanced into Iraq and Syria. They defeated a Byzantine army at Ajnadayn in 634 and took Damascus, Pella and Emesa (Homs). Both the Byzantine and Sasanian empires were exhausted by their long war with each other.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Emperor Heraclius gathered a large army to recover Syria, drawn from Greeks, Syrians, Mesopotamians and Armenians, with Arab tribal contingents under the Ghassanid Jabalah ibn al-Aiham. Al-Baladhuri portrays many Syrians as hostile to Byzantine rule.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Heraclius aimed to drive the Muslim armies out of Syria. The Muslim commanders gave up dispersed positions and concentrated their forces to meet his army in one place.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought near the Yarmuk River (the ancient Hieromax), on a plateau suited to light cavalry and cut by deep wadis. Behind the Byzantine position, the gorge of the Wadi Ruqqad could be crossed by a single bridge.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Vahan, an Armenian general, commanded the Byzantine field army. Abu Ubaidah held the Muslim command; World History Encyclopedia says he ceded battlefield direction to Khalid ibn al-Walid. Al-Baladhuri claims about 200,000 Byzantine troops against 24,000 Muslims; modern estimates are far lower, and no reliable count survives.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Muslim forces withdrew from Palestine, Jordan and Emesa to the Yarmuk plateau and were reinforced from Medina. The armies then faced each other for months of negotiation and build-up before fighting began.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: World History Encyclopedia dates the battle to six days, 15–20 August 636; al-Baladhuri dates it to Rajab of the year 15 AH. After opening duels, Byzantine attacks pushed the Muslim flanks back to their camps, where the women helped rally the men. A cavalry reserve restored the line, and on the last day a Muslim envelopment broke the Byzantine army.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: According to World History Encyclopedia, Khalid refused a truce Vahan requested on the fifth day, sent cavalry at night to seize the bridge over the Wadi Ruqqad and then led massed cavalry around the Byzantine left.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Holding the only bridge in the Byzantine rear turned a defeat into the destruction of the army, since the flank attack drove it toward ground with no escape.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Byzantine army was destroyed; survivors fled toward Palestine, Antioch, Aleppo, Mesopotamia and Armenia. Al-Baladhuri reports that Heraclius left Antioch for Constantinople and bade farewell to Syria.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Syria passed permanently to the caliphate, and Jerusalem surrendered in 637. Al-Baladhuri describes the people of Hims opening their gates and paying tribute. Khalid was removed from command soon after his victory.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A mobile reserve and control of the enemy's line of retreat can matter more than numbers. Local attitudes to imperial rule shaped what followed the battle.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Al-Baladhuri died around 892, so the detailed narratives come from two centuries after the battle, and Arab chroniclers tended to inflate enemy numbers. The sources differ on Jabalah: al-Baladhuri places him with the Byzantines and has him convert only later, while some accounts report a defection during the battle. Vahan's fate is uncertain.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Al-Baladhuri's Futuh al-Buldan gives an early Islamic account built from episodes and anecdotes. World History Encyclopedia gives a modern reconstruction drawing on works such as David Nicolle's study of the battle.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By 1187 Saladin had made the recovery of Jerusalem a central aim. The Latin kingdom of Jerusalem under King Guy of Lusignan was divided by rivalries among its nobles.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Saladin gathered a large army east of the Jordan. Guy, now reconciled with Count Raymond III of Tripoli, assembled the kingdom's forces at the springs of Saffuriya with the Templars, Hospitallers and leading barons, using money from Henry II of England to hire mercenaries.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Saladin besieged Tiberias on 2 July, while the Countess Eschiva held out in the citadel and appealed for help. Guy's council resolved to march to relieve the town. Saladin's aim of drawing the army away from water is an interpretation of his actions, not a documented intention.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Between Saffuriya and the lake of Tiberias lay dry ground in high summer. The army was eventually forced onto the Horns of Hattin, near a village whose water it never reached.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The Frankish army combined the royal host, the military orders and hired troops; De Expugnatione claims 1,200 knights and 18,000 or more infantry. Saladin commanded a large army, and the letter to Archumbald credits Taqi al-Din with the decisive attack.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The army marched in divisions, with Raymond of Tripoli in the vanguard and the Templars in the rearguard. The relic of the True Cross was carried with it by the Bishop of Acre.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On Friday 3 July the army left Saffuriya and its supplies and marched under constant harassment. Short of the lake it halted and camped on dry ground, where the Muslims set fire to the brush around it. At dawn on Saturday 4 July Saladin attacked. The infantry fled to a hilltop, the knights were broken up around the True Cross, and the king was captured.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: De Expugnatione says Raymond advised against the march because of heat and lack of water, but Guy followed other counsel. The Lyon Eracles says the Templar master and Reynald of Châtillon urged battle. On 3 July Guy ordered the army to camp rather than push on to the lake.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The halt without water left a thirsty army surrounded overnight, and it could not fight effectively the next morning.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Guy, the Templar master and many knights were captured, and the True Cross was lost. Reynald of Châtillon was killed; the Lyon Eracles says Saladin killed him himself. De Expugnatione reports that captured Templars and Hospitallers were killed. Raymond, Balian of Ibelin and Reynald of Sidon escaped.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Within two months Saladin recovered most of the kingdom's inland cities and ports. Ashkelon fell in September, and Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October 1187.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Relieving a besieged town can draw a field army onto ground of the enemy's choosing. In summer campaigning, water decided the battle before the fighting began.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The Latin accounts disagree on whose advice led the army astray: one Eracles version blames Raymond's proposed turn toward Hattin, another the Templar master and Reynald. De Expugnatione frames the defeat as divine punishment and favours Raymond, and some Latins suspected Raymond and Reynald of Sidon of collusion with Saladin.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: De Expugnatione is a partisan contemporary Latin chronicle. Edbury translates two versions of the Old French continuation of William of Tyre and a letter written less than two months after the battle. Dajani-Shakeel sets Hattin in the context of Saladin's recovery of Jerusalem, drawing on medieval Arabic accounts.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Mongol forces under Hülegü took Baghdad in 1258 and put the last ʿAbbasid caliph to death. They then took Aleppo and Damascus, ending Ayyubid rule in Syria, and by 1260 had reached Gaza.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Mongols demanded the submission of the Mamluk sultan Qutuz; Britannica says he executed their envoy. News of the Great Khan Möngke's death led Hülegü to withdraw with much of his army, leaving his general Kitbuqa in Syria with a smaller force.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Qutuz aimed to defeat the Mongol force in Syria before it could be reinforced. Kitbuqa had to hold the newly conquered lands with reduced strength.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Ain Jalut (Goliath's Spring) lay in the Jezreel Valley, beneath wooded hills where troops could be concealed. Beisan lay about 13 km away.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Kitbuqa's army included Syrian, Georgian and Armenian troops. Qutuz led the Mamluk army, with Baybars among his generals. Britannica describes the armies as roughly matched; EBSCO calls the Mamluk army vastly superior.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The Mamluks positioned themselves so that the Mongols faced the rising sun and concealed much of their army in the hills. Kitbuqa kept his Syrian troops in reserve, fearing they might defect.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The Mamluk army left Egypt in late July 1260, defeated a small Mongol force at Gaza and passed through Frankish territory near Acre. On 3 September a Mamluk advance force provoked the Mongols and drew them into an ambush. The Mongols broke the Mamluk left wing, but the Mamluks rallied, Kitbuqa fell and the Mongols retreated to Beisan, where they were defeated again.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The Franks of Acre declared neutrality and let the Mamluks pass and resupply, after a clash at Sidon had turned them against the Mongols. Kitbuqa chose to pursue the Mamluk advance force into the valley. Contemporary accounts say Qutuz threw down his helmet and rallied his men when the left wing gave way.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The ambush brought the concealed Mamluk army into action, and the rally after the left wing broke prevented a Mongol breakthrough. The defection of the Syrian auxiliaries then tipped the balance.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Kitbuqa was killed in battle or, by another account, captured and beheaded. The Mamluks occupied Damascus and Aleppo and drove the Mongols out of Syria.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Mamluk rule extended from Egypt to the Euphrates. Qutuz was murdered on the way back to Cairo by a conspiracy formed by Baybars, who seized power. Mongol campaigns into Syria continued in later decades, and Mamluk offensives later took the remaining Frankish strongholds, ending with Acre in 1291.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Events far from the battlefield, such as a succession crisis, can change the balance of forces in a theatre. Knowledge of the ground can turn a familiar tactic against its masters.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources disagree on who directed the battle, Qutuz or Baybars, and on whether the Mamluk retreat was feigned or a regrouping. They also give different balances of strength and different accounts of Kitbuqa's death. Britannica's claim that the battle saved Islam is a strong retrospective judgement.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives a narrative of the battle based on contemporary accounts. The EBSCO research starter gives political context, including the Frankish position, but contains some evident date errors, so it is used here only where it is consistent with Britannica.

sources.title: The Siege of Constantinople in 1453, according to Kritovoulos (trans. Charles T. Riggs, 1954)
The Siege of Constantinople in 1453, according to Nicolo Barbaro (trans. John Melville-Jones, 1969)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: By the mid-15th century the Byzantine Empire held little more than Constantinople and the land just west of it, and the city's population had fallen to perhaps 40,000–50,000. The Ottomans controlled almost all of the Balkans and most of Anatolia, and Murad II had already besieged the city in 1422 before turning to a rebellion elsewhere.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Mehmed II, sultan again from 1451, made peace with Hungary and Venice in 1452 and built a fortress at the narrowest point of the Bosporus. Constantine XI appealed to the West. Hungary refused, and the pope pressed for church union, which the city's people resisted. Venice and Genoa sent help; 700 Genoese under Giovanni Giustiniani Longo arrived in January 1453, and Constantine gave him command of the land defences.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Mehmed meant to blockade the city by land and sea and batter its walls with cannon until he could break in or force a surrender before help came from Christian Europe. Constantine meant to hold the walls until that relief arrived.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The land walls ran about 6.5 km as a double line of ramparts behind a moat and had never been breached. Sea walls lined the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara, and a chain closed the mouth of the Horn. Kritovoulos says a long stretch of wall along the Horn, inside the chain, was left unguarded.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Estimates differ widely. Britannica cites the eyewitness Jacopo Tedaldi for 6,000–7,000 trained soldiers and 30,000–35,000 armed civilians in the city, against 60,000–80,000 Ottoman troops with 69 cannon and a fleet under Baltaoğlu Süleyman Bey. Barbaro puts the sultan's army at about 160,000. Mehmed commanded in person; Giustiniani led the land defence under Constantine.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Kritovoulos says Mehmed divided the walls among his commanders: Zaganos at Galata and the Horn, Karaja, Ishak and Mahmud on sections of the land wall, the sultan with his guard in the centre and Baltaoğlu with the fleet. Giustiniani concentrated most defenders on the land walls, and Barbaro records nine large ships placed along the boom on 9 April.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The bombardment began on 6 April, and an assault the next day was repelled. About 20 April a small relief convoy fought its way through the Ottoman fleet into the harbour. By 22 April Ottoman vessels had been hauled overland into the Golden Horn. Through May the besiegers mined under the walls while the defenders countermined. The general assault began before dawn on 29 May.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: After his fleet failed to force the chain, Mehmed had his smaller ships dragged on greased slipways over the hill behind Galata and into the Horn, stretching the defenders along yet more wall. For the final attack he combined artillery, infantry and ships, and sent in his Janissaries after two waves had been thrown back.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The defence broke when Giustiniani was wounded and carried from the walls, and his men left their posts. The sources disagree about how. Britannica says he was hit by gunfire and Kritovoulos says by a crossbow bolt, while Barbaro, a Venetian hostile to the Genoese, presents him as deserting and spreading a false alarm that the Turks were in.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Ottoman troops took the inner wall at the Gate of St Romanus and the city fell on 29 May 1453. A sack followed, which Kritovoulos describes in detail. Mehmed rode to Hagia Sophia and made it a mosque. Accounts of Constantine XI's death differ: Kritovoulos has him fall fighting at the gate, while Barbaro reports only rumours.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Mehmed moved his capital from Edirne to Constantinople, resettled it with people of many faiths and styled himself Caesar of Rome, then campaigned through the Balkans and Greece. Christian Europe lost its eastern buffer and access to the Black Sea.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Walls that had held for a thousand years fell to a combination of sustained bombardment and complete blockade. Once the chain was bypassed, a small garrison was spread too thin, and its cohesion depended on a few leaders.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Each eyewitness writes from a side. Barbaro dwells on the Venetians and blames the Genoese, and Kritovoulos, who served Mehmed, is the Greek account most favourable to the Ottomans. Numbers vary several-fold between sources. Britannica reports that many scholars see the flight of Greek scholars to Italy as marking the end of the Middle Ages; that is a periodisation, not an event.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: This study uses translated extracts from Kritovoulos's History of Mehmed the Conqueror and Nicolo Barbaro's diary, with Britannica for the overall narrative. Other Greek historians of the fall, such as Sphrantzes, Doukas and Chalkokondyles, were not read here.

sources.publisher: Encyclopaedia Britannica (Tamanna Nangia; Babur by T. G. Percival Spear)

sources.title: The Bābur-nāma in English (Memoirs of Bābur), trans. Annette Susannah Beveridge (1922)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Babur, a descendant of Timur and of Genghis Khan, lost his father's principality of Fergana and failed to hold Samarkand against the Uzbeks. He seized Kabul in 1504 and between 1519 and 1524 raided the Punjab four times without gaining a firm hold.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Ibrahim Lodi, sultan of Delhi from 1517, sought a centralised rule that alienated powerful nobles. Daulat Khan Lodi, governor of the Punjab, and Ibrahim's uncle Alam Khan urged Babur to invade a fifth time.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Babur set out in November 1525 to move against Ibrahim, who held Delhi and the dominions of Hindustan. Reports reached Babur that Ibrahim was advancing slowly to meet him, halting for days at each camp.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Panipat lies about 80 km north of Delhi. Babur rested his right on the town and its suburbs, put carts and mantelets across his front and protected his left with a ditch and felled branches. Gaps an arrow's flight apart let out 100 to 200 horsemen at a time.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Babur reports that Ibrahim's army was estimated at 100,000 men with about 1,000 elephants; Britannica's Babur article gives 100 elephants. Beveridge notes that Babur's army was 12,000 when it crossed the Indus, with later additions in the Punjab, and Babur says a count before the battle fell short of expectations.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Seven hundred carts were joined in the Ottoman fashion with rawhide ropes, with mantelets between them for matchlockmen. Humayun led the right and Muhammad Sultan Mirza the left, with a centre, an advance guard and a reserve. Turning parties (tulughma) stood at the tips of both wings to ride round the enemy's rear.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Humayun defeated Hamid Khan in February 1526, and on 2 April a detachment under Daud Khan Lodi was routed. Babur reached Panipat on 12 April and for a week harassed Ibrahim's camp; a night attack failed. On 20 April Ibrahim advanced at first light and by noon his army was broken. Babur reached Delhi on 24 April and Agra on 4 May.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: A council chose to fight from a fortified position anchored on the town. Babur then tried to provoke Ibrahim with raids and a night attack. When the enemy came on, he reinforced his right and ordered the turning parties to wheel round both flanks while the wings closed in.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: In Babur's account, Ibrahim's army halted on seeing the prepared line, unable either to stand or to keep advancing. The turning parties reached its rear, and its wings were crowded into the centre so tightly that they could neither attack nor escape.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Ibrahim was killed and his body was found among the dead that afternoon. Babur sent columns at once to secure the treasuries of Delhi and Agra, and the Friday sermon was read in his name in Delhi on 27 April.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The battle ended the Lodi dynasty and the Delhi sultanate and set the base for Mughal rule. Unlike Timur, Babur stayed; he persuaded reluctant followers to remain and faced Rana Sanga at Khanua in March 1527.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A smaller army chose its ground, fortified it and let a larger one attack. Field defences, mobile flanking forces and missile fire worked together against an army whose commander could not rely on his nobles.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Babur dates the battle to 20 April; Britannica notes that some scholars prefer 21 April. The role of guns is disputed. Britannica stresses artillery, but Beveridge argues that Babur had few guns, perhaps only two, and that he presents the victory as an archers' success. Babur's portrait of Ibrahim as miserly and untried is the victor's.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The main source is Babur's own memoir, written in Turki, in Beveridge's annotated translation, which compares manuscripts and earlier translations. Her notes also report an Afghan tradition that the fighting was unusually desperate. Britannica supplies the wider context.

sources.title: The battle of Sekigahara – what went right?

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Toyotomi Hideyoshi completed the unification of Japan in 1590. Before his death in 1598 he appointed five regents to rule for his young son Hideyori: Uesugi Kagekatsu, Mōri Terumoto, Maeda Toshiie, Ukita Hideie and Tokugawa Ieyasu.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Ieyasu's political marriages and his move to Ōsaka Castle led others to fear that he meant to supplant the heir. Ishida Mitsunari formed a coalition and on 22 August 1600 denounced him; Ieyasu answered with war. Alliances fell largely along east–west lines, but Uesugi in the east had plotted with Mitsunari.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Mitsunari aimed to preserve the Toyotomi legacy and stop Ieyasu. His plan was to hold the eastern army in the valley and then signal forces on the surrounding heights to descend and trap it. Ieyasu aimed to break the coalition and reunite his three columns in Mino province.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Sekigahara was a village in a mountain valley where several major roads met. Kobayakawa Hideaki's troops held Mount Matsuo to the south, and Mōri and Chōsokabe forces held Mount Nangū behind the eastern army. A thick fog covered the valley until about 8 a.m.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Britannica gives Ieyasu nearly 89,000 men against just under 82,000 for the western coalition, including 15,000 under Kobayakawa. Both armies were coalitions of daimyō under their own lords. Turnbull warns that the standard troop layouts derive from an 1893 General Staff reconstruction based on cruder old maps.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: The western army arrived first after a night withdrawal from Ōgaki Castle. Ukita held the centre, Shimazu Yoshihiro the north and Ōtani Yoshitsugu the south, with Mitsunari behind field fortifications. Ieyasu entered from the Nakasendō road with Fukushima Masanori in the vanguard and Ii Naomasa's shock troops.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Ieyasu's columns converged on Mino; Gifu fell, but his son Hidetada was delayed besieging Ueda Castle. On 21 October fighting began when the fog lifted. At 11 a.m. Mitsunari signalled Kobayakawa, who stayed still until shortly after noon and then attacked Ōtani. Other units defected, the western centre broke, Shimazu withdrew, and by 2 p.m. Ieyasu declared victory.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Ieyasu attacked into a valley overlooked by enemy forces because he had secret assurances from Kobayakawa and Kikkawa Hiroie. Ōtani turned half his men to face Kobayakawa in expectation of betrayal. Kikkawa's refusal to move held back the Mōri and Chōsokabe troops behind him.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Kobayakawa's attack on Ōtani and the defections that followed broke the western line, and Kikkawa's inaction held back some 20,000 Mōri and Chōsokabe troops. Shiramine Jun, as reported by Turnbull, argues that the defection came at the start of the battle rather than at midday.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The western coalition was shattered. Mitsunari fled into the mountains and was beheaded in Kyōto within a month, and Ieyasu took Sawayama and Ōsaka castles within days.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Ieyasu confiscated lands from opponents and rewarded allies, including Kobayakawa and Kikkawa. In 1603 the emperor appointed him shōgun, founding a shogunate that lasted until 1868.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: The battle was largely decided by negotiation before it began; a plan that depended on allies obeying a signal was only as strong as their loyalty. Turnbull also stresses that it was one battle in a wider war, in which events at Fushimi, Gifu and in the north could have changed the result.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Turnbull reports Shiramine Jun's 2014 revision: early reports called the battle Yamanaka, the labels Eastern and Western army appear only in 1698, the story of Ieyasu firing on Kobayakawa is a myth, the hill units were waiting on events, and the battle was shorter. Turnbull finds the defection timing persuasive; Britannica follows the conventional account.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the conventional narrative and Turnbull summarises recent Japanese research. Shiramine's book and the Japanese primary sources were not read directly.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Gustav II Adolf of Sweden fought Poland through the 1620s for land on the Baltic. After the Truce of Altmark in 1629 he landed near Stralsund on 6 July 1630. That summer the emperor's Catholic allies forced the dismissal of Wallenstein and the reduction of his army.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The emperor and his allies refused concessions on the Edict of Restitution, which drove reluctant German Protestants towards Sweden, whose army grew with French and Dutch subsidies. The sack of Magdeburg in May 1631 had dashed Protestant hopes. On 15 September the Swedish army joined that of the Electorate of Saxony.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Gustavus wanted a victory that would persuade other Protestant states to join him. Tilly, who had just taken Leipzig, intended according to Rickard to wait for reinforcements, but his deputy Pappenheim pressed for battle.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The armies met on a plain near the village of Breitenfeld, north of Leipzig. The 1911 Britannica describes a low east–west ridge between Göbschelwitz and Breitenfeld, held by the imperialists, with the allies opposite beyond villages along the Loberbach stream.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Britannica gives 23,000 Swedes and 16,000 Saxons against Tilly's 35,000, and Swedish guns outnumbering imperial guns 51 to 27. The 1911 edition gives about 22,000 Swedes, 15,000 Saxons and at least 32,000 imperialists; Rickard gives 42,000 allies against 36,000. The Saxons were commanded by their elector with Arnim; Pappenheim and Fürstenberg led Tilly's cavalry wings.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Tilly drew up his infantry in large blocks with cavalry on the wings and artillery in front. Gustavus formed two lines with a reserve, mixing pikemen and musketeers in smaller units and attaching musketeers to his cavalry. The raw Saxon army, formed like Tilly's, stood separately on the Swedish left.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: An artillery exchange ran from noon to about 2 p.m. Pappenheim's cavalry then attacked the Swedish right and was driven off. The imperial right broke the Saxons, who fled the field. Tilly's infantry turned on the exposed Swedish left, which re-formed to meet it. About 5 p.m. Gustavus counterattacked, and imperial resistance ended at dusk.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Gustavus kept his lines apart from the Saxons and held a second line and reserve. When the Saxons fled, he used them to form a new left flank instead of retreating. His right wing then wheeled, captured Tilly's guns and turned them on the imperial infantry.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Saxon collapse seemed to open the Swedish flank, but the Swedish formation could change front quickly while Tilly's large blocks could not. The loss of the imperial artillery to the counterattack turned a stalemate into a rout.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The imperial army fled at dusk, with Tilly badly wounded; Rickard credits Pappenheim's cavalry with covering the retreat. Many of the imperial troops who surrendered, mostly mercenaries, enlisted with the Swedes.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: It was the first major Protestant victory of the war. The Swedes overran much of central Germany and Bohemia over the winter of 1631–32 and occupied Bavaria the next summer. Gustavus was hailed as the Lion of the North and drew several Protestant states into alliance, before dying at Lützen in November 1632.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A coalition army is only as strong as its least reliable part, but reserves and flexible formations can absorb the loss of a wing. Artillery placed forward can be captured and used against its owners.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Force figures vary by several thousand between sources. They also differ on the opening: Britannica says a Swedish outflanking move provoked Pappenheim's charge, while the 1911 edition and Rickard simply have Pappenheim open the fighting. Britannica's verdict that the battle proved linear tactics superior is an interpretation.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica's battle article and its history of Europe give the narrative and context, the 1911 Britannica the fullest account of the deployments, and Rickard a concise summary. No contemporary account was read for this study.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: In the War of the Spanish Succession (1702–13) a Franco-Bavarian army threatened Vienna and the Austrian position in Germany. To prevent an Austrian collapse, the Duke of Marlborough marched an army from the Low Countries to the Danube, unnoticed by the French, and joined Prince Eugene of Savoy's Austrian army.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: England, Austria and the Dutch Republic were allied against Louis XIV, while the elector of Bavaria fought on the French side. Losing Vienna would have threatened the alliance itself.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Marlborough and Eugene aimed to save Vienna by defeating the Franco-Bavarian army. Marshal Tallard, expecting them to stay on the defensive to protect Vienna, did not think their slightly smaller army would attack.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Blenheim (now Blindheim) lies on the Danube about 16 km south-west of Donauwörth, where the road to Ulm passes between hills and the marshy river valley. The French front ran along the Nebel stream, covered by the villages of Blenheim, Unterglau and Oberglau, with its left in the hills near Lutzingen.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Britannica gives about 52,000 British, Dutch and Austrian troops under Marlborough and Eugene against about 60,000 French and Bavarians. The French army was in two nearly independent parts: Tallard commanded the right, and Marshal Marsin and the elector the left.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Tallard placed a large force of his best infantry in Blenheim and his cavalry on the wings. The junction between his army and Marsin's was held by cavalry with little infantry support. Marlborough faced Tallard, and Eugene faced Marsin and the elector.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Marlborough and Eugene joined on 12 August and advanced next morning over broken ground cut by streams. The battle opened about 12:30 p.m. Lord Cutts made two failed assaults on Blenheim while Eugene kept Marsin engaged. Marlborough then crossed the Nebel, his cavalry broke the French centre and wheeled against Tallard's wing, and the troops in Blenheim were surrounded.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: The allies chose to attack a larger army in a strong position. Cutts's attacks drew more French reserves into Blenheim than Tallard intended. Marlborough made his main effort against the weak centre, helped by a cavalry corps that Eugene lent him.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The allied cavalry broke through at the junction of the two French armies, separating Marsin from Tallard. With Tallard's infantry packed into Blenheim, his centre had too little to stop the attack.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Tallard was captured and his army almost destroyed, many of its men driven into the Danube. The infantry and dragoons trapped in Blenheim surrendered, while Marsin and the elector withdrew in the dusk.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The battle saved Vienna, preserved the alliance and knocked Bavaria out of the war. Britannica calls it the first major defeat of a French army in over 50 years. It began a lasting partnership between Marlborough and Eugene, and Queen Anne rewarded Marlborough with the manor of Woodstock and funds for Blenheim Palace.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Allied commanders who coordinated closely could defeat a larger army whose two halves fought almost separately. Attacks that pin an enemy's strongpoints can draw away the reserves needed elsewhere.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Figures differ: the 1911 Britannica calls the French only somewhat superior in numbers, and the battalions trapped in Blenheim are given as about 23 or 24. The National Army Museum lists Prussians in the alliance, while Britannica names British, Dutch and Austrian troops. Verdicts such as ending the illusion of French invincibility are judgments.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives the main narrative and the 1911 edition the timings and deployments. The National Army Museum's page interprets John Wootton's painting, made about 40 years after the battle. No contemporary account was read.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: John Burgoyne proposed, and the King and Cabinet approved, a plan for 1777: Burgoyne would march south from Canada and Sir William Howe north from New York to meet at Albany, while Barry St. Leger moved east along the Mohawk from Oswego.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Control of the Hudson–Champlain route would cut New England off from the other colonies. But Howe moved against Philadelphia instead, and the handbook says the order for him to cooperate was apparently never sent.

refs.locator: The British Plan of 1777; Retreat and Surrender

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Burgoyne aimed to reach Albany. The Americans aimed to stop him at Bemis Heights, where their line blocked the river road south.

refs.locator: The Battle of Bennington; The American Line

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Bluffs, ravines and heavy forest covered the ground in 1777. The American line, designed by Thaddeus Kosciuszko, was anchored on the river bluffs and left only a narrow corridor along the river. The woods north of it hindered coordinated attacks and the use of artillery.

refs.locator: The American Line; Guide to the Park

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: The handbook gives Burgoyne about 9,400 men at the start, about half British and half German with several hundred Canadians, Loyalists and Native allies, but elsewhere about 8,500. Horatio Gates replaced Philip Schuyler on 19 August, and his army grew from about 3,000 to 9,000 at Bemis Heights, with Daniel Morgan's riflemen in Benedict Arnold's division.

refs.locator: The Burgoyne Campaign; Retreat of the Americans; The American Line

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Burgoyne crossed the Hudson at Saratoga on 13 September, cutting his communications with Canada. On 19 September he advanced in three columns: Simon Fraser on the right, Burgoyne in the centre and Friedrich Riedesel on the river road with the artillery and baggage.

refs.locator: The Battle of Bennington; The Battle of September 19

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Burgoyne took Ticonderoga in early July but needed until 30 July to reach Fort Edward. A raid for supplies was defeated at Bennington on 16 August. On 19 September the British held the field at Freeman's Farm at heavy cost. On 7 October a British reconnaissance in force was defeated, and on 17 October Burgoyne surrendered.

refs.locator: The Burgoyne Campaign to Retreat and Surrender

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Schuyler slowed the British by felling trees across the roads and stripping the country. On 19 September Gates accepted Arnold's argument for fighting in the woods and sent out Morgan, but held about 5,000 men back. On 7 October Burgoyne sent about 1,500 men to probe the American left, and Gates ordered Morgan, Poor and Learned to attack.

refs.locator: Retreat of the Americans; The Battle of September 19; The Battle of October 7

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The handbook judges that Riedesel's arrival late on 19 September saved the British line. On 7 October the capture of the Breymann Redoubt, which covered the right and rear of Burgoyne's camp, forced a general retreat.

refs.locator: The Battle of September 19; The Battle of October 7

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Burgoyne retreated to Saratoga, where an American force grown to about 20,000 surrounded him. With provisions nearly gone, he surrendered on 17 October under a convention that his troops would be shipped to England. Congress did not keep the terms, and the prisoners were held in America.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: News of the surrender reached France's foreign minister, Vergennes, in December 1777. Hearing of possible British peace offers, he decided not to wait for Spain, and on 6 February 1778 France signed treaties of alliance and of commerce with the United States.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A plan of converging columns failed when one column went elsewhere and another was turned back. An invading army far from its supplies, in country stripped before it, steadily weakened while its opponent grew.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The handbook, written in 1950, spreads the blame across Germain, Howe, Clinton, St. Leger and Burgoyne's lack of drive. It credits Arnold, Morgan and militia mobilisation, and says Fraser was perhaps shot by a marksman Morgan assigned. Its own figures for Burgoyne's army do not agree.

refs.locator: The Battle of October 7; Retreat and Surrender

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The main source is an older National Park Service handbook, read section by section. The Office of the Historian essay, from a series no longer maintained, covers the French alliance. No British, German or American participant accounts were read.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After defeats at Mars-la-Tour and Gravelotte in August 1870, Marshal Bazaine's army was besieged in Metz. Marshal MacMahon's Army of Châlons was the only French army left in the field.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Britannica says Napoleon III, ill and in severe pain, could not fall back on Paris because such an admission of failure would doom his dynasty. The emperor accompanied the army but MacMahon held command.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: MacMahon advanced north towards the Belgian border, intending to turn south-east and relieve Metz. The Germans under Helmuth von Moltke knew of his intentions and moved to intercept him.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Sedan was a small fortress town on the Meuse that could neither feed nor hold the army. Heights surrounded it, from Frénois, where King Wilhelm and Bismarck watched, to the Plateau d'Illy in the north; Bazeilles lay to the south-east.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: About 120,000 French troops faced more than 200,000 Germans; the Fondation Napoléon gives nearly 600 French and 800 German guns. Two German armies, under the Crown Prince of Prussia and Prince Albert of Saxony, closed on the town.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: MacMahon's corps gathered around the citadel. Marine infantry held Bazeilles, and General Margueritte's reserve cavalry stood on the Plateau d'Illy.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: After clashes at Nouart, Beaumont and Bazeilles on 29–31 August, MacMahon fell back into Sedan. Early on 1 September Bavarian troops attacked Bazeilles and MacMahon was badly wounded. Command passed in confusion between Ducrot and Wimpffen while German armies closed the ring, and French cavalry charged in vain to break it.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Ducrot ordered a retreat westward towards Mézières. Wimpffen, claiming authority from the war minister, countermanded him and attacked towards Bazeilles to open a road east. Late in the day Napoleon refused to lead a final breakout, judging that it would only bring pointless slaughter.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: MacMahon's wound left the army under three commanders in a few hours, with conflicting orders and few maps, while German artillery ringed the town. The Fondation Napoléon attributes the disaster largely to this breakdown in communication.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: A white flag was raised and Napoleon offered his sword to King Wilhelm. Moltke and Bismarck demanded unconditional surrender, which Wimpffen signed on 2 September. The army went into captivity and the emperor was held at Wilhelmshöhe.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: When the news reached Paris, a popular uprising overthrew the Second Empire, and the Republic was proclaimed on 4 September. The new government would not accept German terms, and the war went on for five more months.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An operation driven by dynastic politics led an army into a place it could not supply or hold. A command that changed hands mid-battle could not carry out any single plan.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The two accounts disagree on the timing of the white flag: Britannica says early on 2 September, the Fondation Napoléon on the afternoon of 1 September. They name different breakout routes and describe the emperor's surrender differently. Their figures for prisoners also differ.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica's article and the Fondation Napoléon's account, which draws on French and German scholarship, are the sources read. No primary accounts were read.

sources.title: Voyage to Tsushima
sources.publisher: U.S. Naval Institute, Naval History (Capt. Shannon R. Butler)

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Russia and Japan both sought dominance in Manchuria and Korea. On 8 February 1904 Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō's ships attacked the Russian squadron at Port Arthur before Japan's declaration of war, then blockaded the port. The able Russian commander, Admiral Makarov, was killed in April.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Japan had not secured complete command of the sea. In 1904 the tsar decided to send much of the Baltic Fleet, renamed the Second Pacific Squadron, to break the blockade. Port Arthur fell on 2 January 1905, before it arrived.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The squadron was first meant to join the Port Arthur squadron and overwhelm the Japanese navy; after Port Arthur fell, its aim became to reach Vladivostok. Tōgō aimed to intercept and destroy it.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The voyage covered about 18,000 miles with no Russian bases on the way, and French and Portuguese ports turned the squadron away. Admiral Zinovy Rozhestvensky chose the route to Vladivostok through the Tsushima Strait, where Tōgō waited near Pusan on the Korean coast.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Butler counts 38 Russian combatants, including 12 battleships, ranging from very old ships to the newest; many crews had little ocean-going experience. Britannica calls many of the ships old and unserviceable and the Japanese ships superior in speed and armament.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Japanese cruisers shadowed the Russians from early on 27 May. Rozhestvensky tried to form line abreast, but only three battleships managed it, so he reverted to two columns with his four newest battleships on the right.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The squadron left the Baltic in October 1904 and fired on British trawlers off the Dogger Bank. At Nossi-Bé off Madagascar it learned that Port Arthur had fallen, and off Indochina it waited for reinforcements. On 27 May Tōgō's fleet crossed ahead of it and turned, and the leading Russian battleships were quickly disabled. Night torpedo attacks followed, and on 28 May Rear Admiral Nebogatov surrendered.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: After Nossi-Bé, Rozhestvensky proposed returning but went on, expecting reinforcements. He opened fire at 13:49 while the Japanese fleet was turning. Wounded, he was moved to a destroyer; Nebogatov led the remnant north-east, and Rear Admiral Enkvist took his cruisers south to Manila.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Russian gunners missed during the Japanese turn, and Japanese fire soon disabled the leading battleships, including the flagship. With its commander wounded, the battle became a melee that the Russians could not control.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Most of the Russian fleet was sunk, captured or interned. Britannica says four ships reached Vladivostok; Butler says three of 38 combatants eventually did. Nebogatov surrendered the ships still with him.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Within a few hundred miles of its destination, the Baltic Fleet was shattered, and with it Russia's hope of regaining command of the sea. The war ended in disaster for imperial Russia.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A fleet sent across the world without bases arrived worn down before it fought. Butler applies Clausewitz's idea of friction: heat, disease, spoiled food, lack of mail and leave, and exhausting coaling at sea all lowered readiness.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Butler argues that most analyses stress material weaknesses and underrate the human friction of the voyage and Rozhestvensky's leadership. The sources differ on details: the battle is dated 27–28 or 27–29 May, the Dogger Bank incident 21 October or the night of 22–23 October, and the ships reaching Vladivostok as three or four.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Butler draws on Russian participant memoirs and on Westwood, Hough and Pleshakov. Britannica gives a concise summary. No Japanese sources were read. Butler places Vladivostok on Kamchatka, an error not followed here.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: To ease German pressure on France, the Russian commander-in-chief, Grand Duke Nicholas, urged his First and Second Armies into East Prussia before they were fully ready. General Zhilinsky had earlier pledged to France that Russia would field 800,000 men by the 15th day of mobilisation.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: With more than two-to-one superiority, a combined Russian attack could have destroyed the German Eighth Army. But the two army commanders, Rennenkampf and Samsonov, had quarrelled bitterly since the Russo-Japanese War.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Zhilinsky's plan had Rennenkampf's First Army attack from the east to draw the Germans on, while Samsonov's Second Army crossed the southern frontier two days later to cut them off from the Vistula. The Germans aimed to break the invasion.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The 80-km chain of the Masurian Lakes separated the two Russian armies, and the Königsberg fortifications narrowed Rennenkampf's approach. The Russians had left their own border country a barrier of poor railways and worse roads, which now slowed Samsonov.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Rennenkampf had six and a half infantry and five cavalry divisions; Samsonov ten infantry and three cavalry divisions, both under Zhilinsky. The German Eighth Army was commanded by Prittwitz, then by Hindenburg, appointed on 22 August, with Ludendorff as chief of staff and Max Hoffmann on the staff.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Rennenkampf crossed the frontier and pushed back much of the Eighth Army at Gumbinnen on 19–20 August. Samsonov's army, hurried on by Zhilinsky, reached the southern frontier tired, hungry and with its transport incomplete, and spread across a front of nearly 100 km.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 20 August Prittwitz spoke of retreating behind the Vistula, but his staff prepared a move against Samsonov's left; he was replaced two days later. On 26 August François's I Corps attacked near Usdau, and on 27 August the Russian left broke. By 29 August the Germans held the road behind the Russian centre, which surrendered in the forests.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Hoffmann trusted Russian wireless orders sent uncoded, which his superiors suspected were a deception. Ludendorff took the risk of withdrawing almost everything from in front of Rennenkampf, leaving a cavalry screen, to strike both of Samsonov's flanks. Zhilinsky drove Samsonov forward and diverted Rennenkampf towards Königsberg.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: On 27 August the Russian left wing broke under bombardment before the German infantry attacked. François then turned east to Neidenburg, closing the line of retreat of the Russian centre.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Russian centre dissolved into exhausted groups that surrendered in large numbers. Samsonov, caught in the retreat, shot himself; Britannica places this early on 30 August, Rickard probably on 29 August.

refs.locator: Planning and execution; Outcome and aftermath

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Reinforced from the west, the Germans drove Rennenkampf out of East Prussia in September. Britannica notes that they could not turn the victory into a strategic one, and that the corps sent east helped make possible the French recovery on the Marne.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Two armies separated by terrain and unwilling to cooperate could be beaten one at a time. Uncoded radio gave the defender the knowledge to take great risks, and railways let it shift forces quickly.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Britannica gives Hoffmann chief credit for the design and François the essential role, and calls the double envelopment an afterthought rather than a planned second Cannae; Rickard notes that German commanders credited Hindenburg and Ludendorff. Britannica blames Zhilinsky above all, Rickard Samsonov's own push. Dates differ by a day or two.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica gives a detailed narrative and Rickard a short biography of Samsonov. No German or Russian primary sources were read, and the 1914–1918-online encyclopedia article could not be opened.
